text: Make yourself believe the truth of my words,—that certain moments are torn from us, that some are gently removed, and that others glide beyond our reach. The most disgraceful kind of loss, however, is that due to carelessness. Furthermore, if you will pay close heed to the problem, you will find that the largest portion of our life passes while we are doing ill, a goodly share while we are doing nothing, and the whole while we are doing that which is not to the purpose.
note: Wasted time; drifting through life without purpose

tags.when_helps: Someone noticing how much of their time slips away in distraction and carelessness, wanting to take it back.

display_text: Make yourself believe the truth of my words,—that certain moments are torn from us, that some are gently removed, and that others glide beyond our reach. The most disgraceful kind of loss, however, is that due to carelessness. Furthermore, if you will pay close heed to the problem, you will find that the largest portion of our life passes while we are doing ill, a goodly share while we are doing nothing, and the whole while we are doing that which is not to the purpose.
plain: Some of our time is snatched away, some slips off, some drifts out of reach; the most shameful loss is through carelessness. Most of life passes doing wrong, much doing nothing, and all of it doing what doesn't matter.
core_idea: Most of our time is lost through carelessness.

text: What man can you show me who places any value on his time, who reckons the worth of each day, who understands that he is dying daily? For we are mistaken when we look forward to death; the major portion of death has already passed. Whatever years lie behind us are in death’s hands.
note: Valuing each day; mortality

tags.when_helps: Someone who treats time as endless and needs a sober reminder that each passing day is already spent.

display_text: What man can you show me who places any value on his time, who reckons the worth of each day, who understands that he is dying daily? For we are mistaken when we look forward to death; the major portion of death has already passed. Whatever years lie behind us are in death’s hands.
plain: Who truly values his time, weighs each day, and understands that he is dying daily? We wrongly look ahead to death, but most of it is already past: all the years behind us belong to death.
core_idea: We are dying daily; past years belong to death.

text: Lay hold of to-day’s task, and you will not need to depend so much upon to-morrow’s. While we are postponing, life speeds by.
note: Procrastination; acting today

tags.when_helps: Someone procrastinating and worrying about tomorrow's load, who needs a nudge to do today's task now.

display_text: Lay hold of to-day’s task, and you will not need to depend so much upon to-morrow’s. While we are postponing, life speeds by.
plain: Take hold of today's work and you won't need to lean so much on tomorrow. While we put things off, life rushes past.
core_idea: While we postpone, life speeds by.

text: Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time. We were entrusted by nature with the ownership of this single thing, so fleeting and slippery that anyone who will can oust us from possession. What fools these mortals be! They allow the cheapest and most useless things, which can easily be replaced, to be charged in the reckoning, after they have acquired them; but they never regard themselves as in debt when they have received some of that precious commodity,—time! And yet time is the one loan which even a grateful recipient cannot repay.
note: Time as our only true possession

tags.when_helps: Someone who guards money and possessions carefully but lets others and trivial things consume their time.

display_text: Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time. We were entrusted by nature with the ownership of this single thing, so fleeting and slippery that anyone who will can oust us from possession. What fools these mortals be! They allow the cheapest and most useless things, which can easily be replaced, to be charged in the reckoning, after they have acquired them; but they never regard themselves as in debt when they have received some of that precious commodity,—time! And yet time is the one loan which even a grateful recipient cannot repay.
plain: Nothing is truly ours except time, the one thing nature gave us, and it slips away easily. People count cheap, replaceable things as debts, yet never feel indebted for time, the one loan no one can repay.
core_idea: Time is our only true possession.

text: You do not run hither and thither and distract yourself by changing your abode; for such restlessness is the sign of a disordered spirit. The primary indication, to my thinking, of a well-ordered mind is a man’s ability to remain in one place and linger in his own company.
note: Restlessness; being at ease in one's own company

tags.when_helps: Someone who keeps moving, travelling or changing plans to escape unease, and needs to learn to stay with themselves.

display_text: You do not run hither and thither and distract yourself by changing your abode; for such restlessness is the sign of a disordered spirit. The primary indication, to my thinking, of a well-ordered mind is a man’s ability to remain in one place and linger in his own company.
plain: You don't rush around changing where you live, since such restlessness shows a disordered spirit. The first sign of a well-ordered mind is being able to stay in one place and spend time in your own company.
core_idea: A settled mind can stay put and be alone.

text: You must linger among a limited number of master-thinkers, and digest their works, if you would derive ideas which shall win firm hold in your mind. Everywhere means nowhere. When a person spends all his time in foreign travel, he ends by having many acquaintances, but no friends.
note: Depth over breadth; scattered attention

tags.when_helps: Someone spreading themselves thin across many interests or places, with acquaintances everywhere but no deep roots.

display_text: You must linger among a limited number of master-thinkers, and digest their works, if you would derive ideas which shall win firm hold in your mind. Everywhere means nowhere. When a person spends all his time in foreign travel, he ends by having many acquaintances, but no friends.
plain: Stay with a small number of great thinkers and digest their work if you want ideas that take firm root. Being everywhere means being nowhere: someone always travelling ends up with many acquaintances but no friends.
core_idea: Everywhere means nowhere; go deep, not wide.

text: It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor. What does it matter how much a man has laid up in his safe, or in his warehouse, how large are his flocks and how fat his dividends, if he covets his neighbour’s property, and reckons, not his past gains, but his hopes of gains to come? Do you ask what is the proper limit to wealth? It is, first, to have what is necessary, and, second, to have what is enough.
note: Craving more; contentment with enough

tags.when_helps: Someone always wanting more money or comparing with neighbours, unsure where enough lies.

display_text: It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor. What does it matter how much a man has laid up in his safe, or in his warehouse, how large are his flocks and how fat his dividends, if he covets his neighbour’s property, and reckons, not his past gains, but his hopes of gains to come? Do you ask what is the proper limit to wealth? It is, first, to have what is necessary, and, second, to have what is enough.
plain: The poor man isn't the one with too little but the one who craves more. However much you own, coveting your neighbour's goods and future gains makes you poor. The right limit: first what's needed, then what's enough.
core_idea: Poverty is craving more, not having little.

text: But if you consider any man a friend whom you do not trust as you trust yourself, you are mightily mistaken and you do not sufficiently understand what true friendship means. Indeed, I would have you discuss everything with a friend; but first of all discuss the man himself. When friendship is settled, you must trust; before friendship is formed, you must pass judgment. Those persons indeed put last first and confound their duties, who, violating the rules of Theophrastus, judge a man after they have made him their friend, instead of making him their friend after they have judged him. Ponder for a long time whether you shall admit a given person to your friendship; but when you have decided to admit him, welcome him with all your heart and soul. Speak as boldly with him as with yourself.
note: Choosing friends carefully, then trusting fully

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone unsure whether to trust a friend fully, or deciding whom to let into their inner circle.

display_text: But if you consider any man a friend whom you do not trust as you trust yourself, you are mightily mistaken and you do not sufficiently understand what true friendship means. Those persons indeed put last first and confound their duties, who, violating the rules of Theophrastus, judge a man after they have made him their friend, instead of making him their friend after they have judged him. Speak as boldly with him as with yourself.
plain: If you don't trust a friend as you trust yourself, you misunderstand friendship. Judge a person before befriending him, not after. Think long before admitting someone; once you do, welcome him wholeheartedly and speak as freely as to yourself.
core_idea: Judge before befriending; then trust completely.

text: There is a class of men who communicate, to anyone whom they meet, matters which should be revealed to friends alone, and unload upon the chance listener whatever irks them. Others, again, fear to confide in their closest intimates; and if it were possible, they would not trust even themselves, burying their secrets deep in their hearts. But we should do neither. It is equally faulty to trust everyone and to trust no one. Yet the former fault is, I should say, the more ingenuous, the latter the more safe.
note: Oversharing versus trusting no one

tags.when_helps: Someone who either overshares with everyone or confides in no one, looking for a wiser balance of trust.

display_text: There is a class of men who communicate, to anyone whom they meet, matters which should be revealed to friends alone, and unload upon the chance listener whatever irks them. Others, again, fear to confide in their closest intimates; and if it were possible, they would not trust even themselves, burying their secrets deep in their hearts. But we should do neither. plain: Some people pour out private matters to anyone they meet; others won't confide even in their closest friends. Both are wrong: trusting everyone and trusting no one are equal faults, though the first is more innocent and the second safer.
core_idea: Trusting everyone and trusting no one are both faults.

text: For love of bustle is not industry,—it is only the restlessness of a hunted mind. And true repose does not consist in condemning all motion as merely vexation; that kind of repose is slackness and inertia.
note: Busyness versus real work; rest versus inertia

tags.when_helps: Someone who mistakes constant busyness for productivity, or swings into idleness and calls it rest.

display_text: For love of bustle is not industry,—it is only the restlessness of a hunted mind. And true repose does not consist in condemning all motion as merely vexation; that kind of repose is slackness and inertia.
plain: Love of busyness is not hard work; it is only the restlessness of a hunted mind. And true rest isn't rejecting all activity as a nuisance; that kind of rest is just laziness.
core_idea: Busyness is restlessness; idleness isn't rest.

text: No evil is great which is the last evil of all. Death arrives; it would be a thing to dread, if it could remain with you. But death must either not come at all, or else must come and pass away.
note: Fear of death

tags.when_helps: Someone gripped by fear of death who wants a calm argument that it need not be dreaded.

display_text: No evil is great which is the last evil of all. Death arrives; it would be a thing to dread, if it could remain with you. But death must either not come at all, or else must come and pass away.
plain: No evil is great if it is the last one. Death would be worth dreading if it stayed with you, but it either doesn't come at all or comes and passes.
core_idea: Death, the last evil, cannot stay with you.

text: Most men ebb and flow in wretchedness between the fear of death and the hardships of life; they are unwilling to live, and yet they do not know how to die.
note: Caught between fear of death and life's hardship

tags.when_helps: Someone caught between life's hardships and fear of death, who wants to know this tension is common to all.

display_text: Most men ebb and flow in wretchedness between the fear of death and the hardships of life; they are unwilling to live, and yet they do not know how to die.
plain: Most people drift miserably between fear of death and the hardships of life: they don't want to live, and yet they don't know how to die.
core_idea: People fear death yet dislike living.

text: No good thing renders its possessor happy, unless his mind is reconciled to the possibility of loss; nothing, however, is lost with less discomfort than that which, when lost, cannot be missed.
note: Accepting possible loss of what we have

tags.when_helps: Someone who cannot enjoy what they have because they fear losing it.

display_text: No good thing renders its possessor happy, unless his mind is reconciled to the possibility of loss; nothing, however, is lost with less discomfort than that which, when lost, cannot be missed.
plain: No good thing makes its owner happy unless his mind has accepted that he might lose it; and nothing is lost more easily than what, once lost, isn't missed.
core_idea: Accept possible loss to enjoy what you have.

plain_judge.issue: Renders lost with less discomfort as lost more easily, blurring the meaning.

text: No man has ever been so far advanced by Fortune that she did not threaten him as greatly as she had previously indulged him. Do not trust her seeming calm; in a moment the sea is moved to its depths. The very day the ships have made a brave show in the games, they are engulfed.
note: Success is fragile; fortune can turn

tags.when_helps: Someone riding a wave of success who needs a reminder that good fortune can turn without warning.

display_text: No man has ever been so far advanced by Fortune that she did not threaten him as greatly as she had previously indulged him. Do not trust her seeming calm; in a moment the sea is moved to its depths. The very day the ships have made a brave show in the games, they are engulfed.
plain: No one has been raised so high by Fortune that she didn't threaten him as much as she favoured him. Don't trust her calm: the sea can churn in a moment, and proud ships can sink the same day.
core_idea: Fortune's calm can turn in a moment.

text: It is the superfluous things for which men sweat,—the superfluous things that wear our togas threadbare, that force us to grow old in camp, that dash us upon foreign shores. That which is enough is ready to our hands. He who has made a fair compact with poverty is rich.
note: Striving for excess; enough is close at hand

tags.when_helps: Someone working themselves ragged for extras they don't need, who could find relief in wanting less.

display_text: It is the superfluous things for which men sweat,—the superfluous things that wear our togas threadbare, that force us to grow old in camp, that dash us upon foreign shores. That which is enough is ready to our hands. He who has made a fair compact with poverty is rich.
plain: People toil for unnecessary things, which wear out their clothes, keep them in army camps till old age and wreck them on foreign shores. What is enough is close at hand. Whoever has made peace with poverty is rich.
core_idea: Whoever makes peace with poverty is rich.

text: Just as the same chain fastens the prisoner and the soldier who guards him, so hope and fear, dissimilar as they are, keep step together; fear follows hope.
note: Anxious hoping; hope and fear bound together

tags.when_helps: Someone swinging between hoping and fearing about an outcome, who might see the two as linked.

display_text: Just as the same chain fastens the prisoner and the soldier who guards him, so hope and fear, dissimilar as they are, keep step together; fear follows hope.
plain: Just as one chain binds a prisoner to the soldier guarding him, hope and fear, though unlike, march together: fear follows hope.
core_idea: Hope and fear are chained together.

text: Beasts avoid the dangers which they see, and when they have escaped them are free from care; but we men torment ourselves over that which is to come as well as over that which is past. Many of our blessings bring bane to us; for memory recalls the tortures of fear, while foresight anticipates them. The present alone can make no man wretched.
note: Worry about future and past; living in the present

tags.when_helps: Someone tormented by memories and anticipation, who needs reminding that the present moment alone is bearable.

display_text: Beasts avoid the dangers which they see, and when they have escaped them are free from care; but we men torment ourselves over that which is to come as well as over that which is past. Many of our blessings bring bane to us; for memory recalls the tortures of fear, while foresight anticipates them. The present alone can make no man wretched.
plain: Animals flee dangers they see and then stop worrying, but humans torment themselves over the future and the past. Memory brings back fear and foresight anticipates it. The present alone can make no one miserable.
core_idea: Only past and future torment us; the present doesn't.

text: I feel, my dear Lucilius, that I am being not only reformed, but transformed. I do not yet, however, assure myself, or indulge the hope, that there are no elements left in me which need to be changed. Of course there are many that should be made more compact, or made thinner, or be brought into greater prominence. And indeed this very fact is proof that my spirit is altered into something better,—that it can see its own faults, of which it was previously ignorant. In certain cases sick men are congratulated because they themselves have perceived that they are sick.
note: Seeing one's own faults as a sign of growth

tags.when_helps: Someone newly aware of their faults and discouraged by it, who can take that awareness as a sign of growth.

display_text: I feel, my dear Lucilius, that I am being not only reformed, but transformed. I do not yet, however, assure myself, or indulge the hope, that there are no elements left in me which need to be changed. Of course there are many that should be made more compact, or made thinner, or be brought into greater prominence. And indeed this very fact is proof that my spirit is altered into something better,—that it can see its own faults, of which it was previously ignorant. In certain cases sick men are congratulated because they themselves have perceived that they are sick.
plain: Seneca feels not just improved but transformed, though much in him still needs changing. Seeing faults he never noticed proves his spirit is better, just as a sick man who knows he is sick is congratulated.
core_idea: Seeing your faults is a sign of progress.

plain_judge.issue: Recasts first-person confession to Lucilius as third-person report about Seneca.

text: I can show you many who have lacked, not a friend, but a friendship; this, however, cannot possibly happen when souls are drawn together by identical inclinations into an alliance of honourable desires. And why can it not happen? Because in such cases men know that they have all things in common, especially their troubles.
note: True friendship; sharing troubles

tags.when_helps: Someone with plenty of friends but no real friendship, wondering what makes a bond deep.

display_text: I can show you many who have lacked, not a friend, but a friendship; this, however, cannot possibly happen when souls are drawn together by identical inclinations into an alliance of honourable desires. And why can it not happen? Because in such cases men know that they have all things in common, especially their troubles.
plain: Many have lacked not a friend but a friendship. That can't happen when souls are joined by shared, honourable aims, because then people know they hold everything in common, especially their troubles.
core_idea: True friends share everything, especially troubles.

text: Nothing will ever please me, no matter how excellent or beneficial, if I must retain the knowledge of it to myself. And if wisdom were given me under the express condition that it must be kept hidden and not uttered, I should refuse it. No good thing is pleasant to possess, without friends to share it.
note: Joy in sharing good things with friends

tags.when_helps: Someone with good news or a new insight and no one to share it with.

display_text: Nothing will ever please me, no matter how excellent or beneficial, if I must retain the knowledge of it to myself. And if wisdom were given me under the express condition that it must be kept hidden and not uttered, I should refuse it. No good thing is pleasant to possess, without friends to share it.
plain: Nothing pleases me, however good, if I must keep it to myself. If wisdom were offered on condition that I hide it, I'd refuse it. No good thing is pleasant to have without friends to share it.
core_idea: No good is pleasant without friends to share it.

text: “What progress, you ask, have I made? I have begun to be a friend to myself.” That was indeed a great benefit; such a person can never be alone. You may be sure that such a man is a friend to all mankind.
note: Befriending oneself; loneliness

tags.when_helps: Someone feeling alone who could begin by becoming a friend to themselves.

display_text: “What progress, you ask, have I made? I have begun to be a friend to myself.” That was indeed a great benefit; such a person can never be alone. You may be sure that such a man is a friend to all mankind.
plain: Asked what progress he had made, a man answered that he had begun to be a friend to himself. That is a great gain: such a person is never alone, and is surely a friend to all humankind.
core_idea: Befriend yourself and you are never alone.

text: I shall admit my own weakness, at any rate; for I never bring back home the same character that I took abroad with me. Something of that which I have forced to be calm within me is disturbed; some of the foes that I have routed return again.
note: How crowds unsettle a hard-won calm

situations: a habit or addiction I can't break
tags.when_helps: Someone who slips back into old habits after time in a crowd, and needs to know even the wise do.

display_text: I shall admit my own weakness, at any rate; for I never bring back home the same character that I took abroad with me. Something of that which I have forced to be calm within me is disturbed; some of the foes that I have routed return again.
plain: Seneca admits his weakness: he never comes home with the same character he took out. Something he had calmed inside is stirred up again, and some enemies he had beaten come back.
core_idea: Going among crowds unsettles the calm we've built.

text: Much harm is done by a single case of indulgence or greed; the familiar friend, if he be luxurious, weakens and softens us imperceptibly; the neighbour, if he be rich, rouses our covetousness; the companion, if he be slanderous, rubs off some of his rust upon us, even though we be spotless and sincere. What then do you think the effect will be on character, when the world at large assaults it! You must either imitate or loathe the world. But both courses are to be avoided; you should not copy the bad simply because they are many, nor should you hate the many because they are unlike you. Withdraw into yourself, as far as you can. Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve. The process is mutual; for men learn while they teach.
note: Influence of companions; choosing good company

tags.when_helps: Someone worried the people around them are pulling them down, looking for counsel on choosing company.

display_text: Much harm is done by a single case of indulgence or greed; the familiar friend, if he be luxurious, weakens and softens us imperceptibly; the neighbour, if he be rich, rouses our covetousness; the companion, if he be slanderous, rubs off some of his rust upon us, even though we be spotless and sincere. plain: One example of indulgence or greed does great harm; companions rub off on us. Don't copy the bad because they're many, nor hate the many. Withdraw into yourself; keep company with those who improve you and whom you can improve.
core_idea: Keep company that makes you better; we learn by teaching.

plain_judge.issue: Drops the closing point that the process is mutual: people learn while they teach.

text: You may say: “For what purpose did I learn all these things?” But you need not fear that you have wasted your efforts; it was for yourself that you learned them.
note: Effort unrecognised by others is not wasted

tags.when_helps: Someone wondering whether their study or effort was wasted because no one noticed or used it.

display_text: You may say: “For what purpose did I learn all these things?” But you need not fear that you have wasted your efforts; it was for yourself that you learned them.
plain: You may ask why you learned all these things. Don't worry that the effort was wasted: you learned them for yourself.
core_idea: Learning for yourself is never wasted.

text: Many men praise you; but have you any reason for being pleased with yourself, if you are a person whom the many can understand? Your good qualities should face inwards.
note: Seeking approval and applause from others

tags.when_helps: Someone basking in praise or chasing approval, who needs to ask whether they are pleased with themselves.

display_text: Many men praise you; but have you any reason for being pleased with yourself, if you are a person whom the many can understand? Your good qualities should face inwards.
plain: Many people praise you, but should you be pleased with yourself if the crowd can understand you? Your good qualities should face inward.
core_idea: Let your good qualities face inward.

text: Do you call these things the ‘gifts’ of Fortune? They are snares. And any man among you who wishes to live a life of safety will avoid, to the utmost of his power, these limed twigs of her favour, by which we mortals, most wretched in this respect also, are deceived; for we think that we hold them in our grasp, but they hold us in theirs.
note: Possessions and luck that end up owning us

tags.when_helps: Someone tempted by wealth, perks or status, who senses these may own them rather than the reverse.

display_text: Do you call these things the ‘gifts’ of Fortune? They are snares. And any man among you who wishes to live a life of safety will avoid, to the utmost of his power, these limed twigs of her favour, by which we mortals, most wretched in this respect also, are deceived; for we think that we hold them in our grasp, but they hold us in theirs.
plain: Fortune's so-called gifts are traps. Anyone who wants a safe life will avoid her sticky lures as far as he can; we think we hold these things, but they hold us.
core_idea: Fortune's gifts are traps that hold us.

text: Eat merely to relieve your hunger; drink merely to quench your thirst; dress merely to keep out the cold; house yourself merely as a protection against personal discomfort. It matters little whether the house be built of turf, or of variously coloured imported marble; understand that a man is sheltered just as well by a thatch as by a roof of gold. Despise everything that useless toil creates as an ornament and an object of beauty. And reflect that nothing except the soul is worthy of wonder; for to the soul, if it be great, naught is great.
note: Simple living; what truly deserves wonder

tags.when_helps: Someone caught up in wanting a finer home or things, who could find freedom in living simply.

display_text: Eat merely to relieve your hunger; drink merely to quench your thirst; dress merely to keep out the cold; house yourself merely as a protection against personal discomfort. It matters little whether the house be built of turf, or of variously coloured imported marble; understand that a man is sheltered just as well by a thatch as by a roof of gold. Despise everything that useless toil creates as an ornament and an object of beauty. And reflect that nothing except the soul is worthy of wonder; for to the soul, if it be great, naught is great.
plain: Eat to end hunger, drink to quench thirst, dress against cold, house yourself against discomfort; thatch shelters as well as gold. Scorn useless ornament. Only the soul deserves wonder, and to a great soul nothing is great.
core_idea: Meet only real needs; only the soul deserves wonder.

text: Believe me, those who seem to be busied with nothing are busied with the greater tasks; they are dealing at the same time with things mortal and things immortal.
note: Quiet reflective work that looks like idleness

tags.when_helps: Someone judged as idle because their reflective or inner work doesn't look busy to others.

display_text: Believe me, those who seem to be busied with nothing are busied with the greater tasks; they are dealing at the same time with things mortal and things immortal.
plain: Those who seem to be doing nothing are often doing the greater work, dealing with things both mortal and immortal at once.
core_idea: Quiet reflection can be the greatest work.

plain_judge.issue: Adds 'often', softening the claim that the seemingly idle are busied with greater tasks.

text: Hecato, says: “I can show you a philtre, compounded without drugs, herbs, or any witch’s incantation: ‘If you would be loved, love.’” Now there is great pleasure, not only in maintaining old and established friendships, but also in beginning and acquiring new ones.
note: Wanting to be loved; making new friends

keywords: if you would be loved, love
tags.when_helps: Someone longing to be loved or to make new friends, wondering where to start.

display_text: Hecato says: “I can show you a philtre, compounded without drugs, herbs, or any witch’s incantation: ‘If you would be loved, love.’” Now there is great pleasure, not only in maintaining old and established friendships, but also in beginning and acquiring new ones.
plain: Hecato offers a love potion that needs no drugs, herbs or spells: if you want to be loved, love. There is great pleasure both in keeping old friendships and in making new ones.
core_idea: If you would be loved, love.

text: There is the same difference between winning a new friend and having already won him, as there is between the farmer who sows and the farmer who reaps. The philosopher Attalus used to say: “It is more pleasant to make than to keep a friend, as it is more pleasant to the artist to paint than to have finished painting.” When one is busy and absorbed in one’s work, the very absorption affords great delight; but when one has withdrawn one’s hand from the completed masterpiece, the pleasure is not so keen. Henceforth it is the fruits of his art that he enjoys; it was the art itself that he enjoyed while he was painting. In the case of our children, their young manhood yields the more abundant fruits, but their infancy was sweeter.
note: Joy of the process; friendship, work, children growing

tags.when_helps: Someone missing the early sweetness of a friendship or their children's infancy, reflecting on how bonds change.

display_text: There is the same difference between winning a new friend and having already won him, as there is between the farmer who sows and the farmer who reaps. The philosopher Attalus used to say: “It is more pleasant to make than to keep a friend, as it is more pleasant to the artist to paint than to have finished painting.” When one is busy and absorbed in one’s work, the very absorption affords great delight; but when one has withdrawn one’s hand from the completed masterpiece, the pleasure is not so keen. Henceforth it is the fruits of his art that he enjoys; it was the art itself that he enjoyed while he was painting. In the case of our children, their young manhood yields the more abundant fruits, but their infancy was sweeter.
plain: Winning a friend differs from having won one as sowing from reaping. Making a friend pleases more than keeping one, as painting pleases an artist more than the finished picture; so too children's infancy is sweeter than their youth.
core_idea: Making a friend delights more than keeping one.

plain_judge.issue: Drops delight of absorption and that youth yields more fruit; compresses the contrast.

text: These are the so-called “fair-weather” friendships; one who is chosen for the sake of utility will be satisfactory only so long as he is useful. Hence prosperous men are blockaded by troops of friends; but those who have failed stand amid vast loneliness, their friends fleeing from the very crisis which is to test their worth. Hence, also, we notice those many shameful cases of persons who, through fear, desert or betray. The beginning and the end cannot but harmonize. He who begins to be your friend because it pays will also cease because it pays. A man will be attracted by some reward offered in exchange for his friendship, if he be attracted by aught in friendship other than friendship itself.

text: It is a true saying which I have found in Athenodorus: “Know that thou art freed from all desires when thou hast reached such a point that thou prayest to God for nothing except what thou canst pray for openly.” But how foolish men are now! They whisper the basest of prayers to heaven; but if anyone listens, they are silent at once. That which they are unwilling for men to know, they communicate to God. Do you not think, then, that some such wholesome advice as this could be given you: “Live among men as if God beheld you; speak with God as if men were listening”?
note: Hidden desires; living with integrity

text: We can get rid of most sins, if we have a witness who stands near us when we are likely to go wrong. text: Let us cherish and love old age; for it is full of pleasure if one knows how to use it. Fruits are most welcome when almost over; youth is most charming at its close; the last drink delights the toper,—the glass which souses him and puts the finishing touch on his drunkenness.

text: Life is most delightful when it is on the downward slope, but has not yet reached the abrupt decline. text: For our powers can never inspire in us implicit faith in ourselves except when many difficulties have confronted us on this side and on that, and have occasionally even come to close quarters with us. It is only in this way that the true spirit can be tested,—the spirit that will never consent to come under the jurisdiction of things external to ourselves. This is the touchstone of such a spirit; no prizefighter can go with high spirits into the strife if he has never been beaten black and blue; the only contestant who can confidently enter the lists is the man who has seen his own blood, who has felt his teeth rattle beneath his opponent’s fist, who has been tripped and felt the full force of his adversary’s charge, who has been downed in body but not in spirit, one who, as often as he falls, rises again with greater defiance than ever.

text: There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality. I am not speaking with you in the Stoic strain but in my milder style. For it is our Stoic fashion to speak of all those things, which provoke cries and groans, as unimportant and beneath notice; but you and I must drop such great-sounding words, although, Heaven knows, they are true enough. What I advise you to do is, not to be unhappy before the crisis comes; since it may be that the dangers before which you paled as if they were threatening you, will never come upon you; they certainly have not yet come. Accordingly, some things torment us more than they ought; some torment us before they ought; and some torment us when they ought not to torment us at all. We are in the habit of exaggerating, or imagining, or anticipating, sorrow.
note: Anxiety; suffering more in imagination than reality

tags.when_helps: Someone anxiously anticipating trouble that hasn't happened, who needs gentle perspective on imagined suffering.

text: Do me the favour, when men surround you and try to talk you into believing that you are unhappy, to consider not what you hear but what you yourself feel, and to take counsel with your feelings and question yourself independently, because you know your own affairs better than anyone else does. Ask: “Is there any reason why these persons should condole with me? Why should they be worried or even fear some infection from me, as if troubles could be transmitted? Is there any evil involved, or is it a matter merely of ill report, rather than an evil?” Put the question voluntarily to yourself: “Am I tormented without sufficient reason, am I morose, and do I convert what is not an evil into what is an evil?”
note: Others' opinions of our misfortune; self-questioning

tags.when_helps: Someone being told by others that they should feel miserable, who needs to check their own feelings.

text: First of all, consider whether your proofs of future trouble are sure. For it is more often the case that we are troubled by our apprehensions, and that we are mocked by that mocker, rumour, which is wont to settle wars, but much more often settles individuals. Yes, my dear Lucilius; we agree too quickly with what people say. We do not put to the test those things which cause our fear; we do not examine into them; we blench and retreat just like soldiers who are forced to abandon their camp because of a dust-cloud raised by stampeding cattle, or are thrown into a panic by the spreading of some unauthenticated rumour.
note: Fear driven by rumour; testing our worries

tags.when_helps: Someone panicking over rumours or unconfirmed bad news, who should test the evidence before fearing.

text: The mind at times fashions for itself false shapes of evil when there are no signs that point to any evil; it twists into the worst construction some word of doubtful meaning; or it fancies some personal grudge to be more serious than it really is, considering not how angry the enemy is, but to what lengths he may go if he is angry. But life is not worth living, and there is no limit to our sorrows, if we indulge our fears to the greatest possible extent; in this matter, let prudence help you, and contemn with a resolute spirit even when it is in plain sight. If you cannot do this, counter one weakness with another, and temper your fear with hope. There is nothing so certain among these objects of fear that it is not more certain still that things we dread sink into nothing and that things we hope for mock us.
note: Catastrophising; tempering fear with hope

tags.when_helps: Someone whose mind spins worst-case stories from small signs, looking for a way to steady it.

text: I do not maintain that the body is not to be indulged at all; but I maintain that we must not be slaves to it. He will have many masters who makes his body his master, who is over-fearful in its behalf, who judges everything according to the body. We should conduct ourselves not as if we ought to live for the body, but as if we could not live without it. Our too great love for it makes us restless with fears, burdens us with cares, and exposes us to insults. Virtue is held too cheap by the man who counts his body too dear.

text: He who craves riches feels fear on their account. No man, however, enjoys a blessing that brings anxiety; he is always trying to add a little more. While he puzzles over increasing his wealth, he forgets how to use it. plain: You don't need to bend over your books constantly; the mind needs a change, but one that relaxes it without weakening it.

text: When you see many ahead of you, think how many are behind! If you would thank the gods, and be grateful for your past life, you should contemplate how many men you have outstripped. But what have you to do with the others? You have outstripped yourself.
note: Comparing yourself to others; envy; gratitude for progress

tags.when_helps: Someone comparing themselves with those ahead, who could notice how far they themselves have come.

display_text: When you see many ahead of you, think how many are behind! If you would thank the gods, and be grateful for your past life, you should contemplate how many men you have outstripped. But what have you to do with the others? You have outstripped yourself.
plain: When you see many people ahead of you, think how many are behind. To be grateful for your life, consider how many you have passed. But why bother with others? You have surpassed yourself.
core_idea: Measure progress against yourself, not others.

plain_judge.issue: Drops thanking the gods; gratitude rendered without its religious frame.

text: Fix a limit which you will not even desire to pass, should you have the power. At last, then, away with all these treacherous goods! They look better to those who hope for them than to those who have attained them. If there were anything substantial in them, they would sooner or later satisfy you; as it is, they merely rouse the drinkers' thirst.
note: Endless wanting; ambition that never satisfies

tags.when_helps: Someone who keeps reaching for more yet feels emptier after each gain, needing to set a limit.

display_text: Fix a limit which you will not even desire to pass, should you have the power. At last, then, away with all these treacherous goods! They look better to those who hope for them than to those who have attained them. If there were anything substantial in them, they would sooner or later satisfy you; as it is, they merely rouse the drinkers' thirst.
plain: Set a limit you won't even want to pass. Away with deceptive goods: they look better to those hoping for them than to those who have them. If they had substance they'd satisfy; instead they make the drinker thirstier.
core_idea: Set a limit; worldly goods never satisfy.

text: It is clear to you, I am sure, Lucilius, that no man can live a happy life, or even a supportable life, without the study of wisdom; you know also that a happy life is reached when our wisdom is brought to completion, but that life is at least endurable even when our wisdom is only begun. This idea, however, clear though it is, must be strengthened and implanted more deeply by daily reflection; it is more important for you to keep the resolutions you have already made than to go on and make noble ones. You must persevere, must develop new strength by continuous study, until that which is only a good inclination becomes a good settled purpose.
note: Keeping resolutions; turning good intentions into habit

tags.when_helps: Someone who has started trying to live wisely and needs encouragement to keep going rather than make new vows.

display_text: It is clear to you, I am sure, Lucilius, that no man can live a happy life, or even a supportable life, without the study of wisdom; you know also that a happy life is reached when our wisdom is brought to completion, but that life is at least endurable even when our wisdom is only begun. plain: No one can live happily, or even bearably, without studying wisdom; completed wisdom brings happiness, begun wisdom makes life bearable. Keeping the resolutions you've made matters more than making grand new ones; persevere until good inclination becomes settled purpose.
core_idea: Keep your resolutions until they become character.

text: Philosophy is no trick to catch the public; it is not devised for show. It is a matter, not of words, but of facts. It is not pursued in order that the day may yield some amusement before it is spent, or that our leisure may be relieved of a tedium that irks us. It moulds and constructs the soul; it orders our life, guides our conduct, shows us what we should do and what we should leave undone; it sits at the helm and directs our course as we waver amid uncertainties. Without it, no one can live fearlessly or in peace of mind. Countless things that happen every hour call for advice; and such advice is to be sought in philosophy.
note: Needing guidance amid uncertainty; living wisely

tags.when_helps: Someone wavering amid uncertainty, who wants a guide for everyday choices rather than entertainment.

display_text: Philosophy is no trick to catch the public; it is not devised for show. It is a matter, not of words, but of facts. plain: Philosophy isn't a show or a pastime; it is deeds, not words. It shapes the soul, orders life, guides conduct and steers us through uncertainty. Without it no one lives fearlessly or at peace.
core_idea: Philosophy shapes the soul and steers life.

text: Natural desires are limited; but those which spring from false opinion can have no stopping-point. The false has no limits. When you are travelling on a road, there must be an end; but when astray, your wanderings are limitless. Recall your steps, therefore, from idle things, and when you would know whether that which you seek is based upon a natural or upon a misleading desire, consider whether it can stop at any definite point. If you find, after having travelled far, that there is a more distant goal always in view, you may be sure that this condition is contrary to nature.
note: Telling real needs from endless craving

tags.when_helps: Someone whose goals keep moving further away, wanting a test for which desires are worth following.

display_text: Natural desires are limited; but those which spring from false opinion can have no stopping-point. The false has no limits. When you are travelling on a road, there must be an end; but when astray, your wanderings are limitless. Recall your steps, therefore, from idle things, and when you would know whether that which you seek is based upon a natural or upon a misleading desire, consider whether it can stop at any definite point. If you find, after having travelled far, that there is a more distant goal always in view, you may be sure that this condition is contrary to nature.
plain: Natural desires have limits; desires born of false opinion have none. A road ends, but wandering doesn't. To tell natural desire from misleading desire, ask whether it can stop somewhere; if the goal keeps receding, it is against nature.
core_idea: Natural desires have limits; false ones never end.

text: That which had made poverty a burden to us, has made riches also a burden. Just as it matters little whether you lay a sick man on a wooden or on a golden bed, for whithersoever he be moved he will carry his malady with him; so one need not care whether the diseased mind is bestowed upon riches or upon poverty. His malady goes with the man.
note: Unhappiness lies in the mind, not circumstances or money

tags.when_helps: Someone sure that more money would end their unhappiness, who might see the trouble lies in the mind.

display_text: That which had made poverty a burden to us, has made riches also a burden. Just as it matters little whether you lay a sick man on a wooden or on a golden bed, for whithersoever he be moved he will carry his malady with him; so one need not care whether the diseased mind is bestowed upon riches or upon poverty. His malady goes with the man.
plain: Whatever made poverty hard also makes wealth hard. A sick man is sick on any bed, and a troubled mind stays troubled whether it is rich or poor; the illness travels with the person.
core_idea: A troubled mind stays troubled, rich or poor.

text: It shows much more courage to remain dry and sober when the mob is drunk and vomiting; but it shows greater self-control to refuse to withdraw oneself and to do what the crowd does, but in a different way,—thus neither making oneself conspicuous nor becoming one of the crowd. For one may keep holiday without extravagance.
note: Keeping your own standards amid peer pressure

tags.when_helps: Someone at a party or holiday who wants to stay moderate without making a show of standing apart.

display_text: It shows much more courage to remain dry and sober when the mob is drunk and vomiting; but it shows greater self-control to refuse to withdraw oneself and to do what the crowd does, but in a different way,—thus neither making oneself conspicuous nor becoming one of the crowd. For one may keep holiday without extravagance.
plain: It takes courage to stay sober while the crowd gets drunk, but more self-control to join in the festival in your own restrained way, neither standing out nor losing yourself in the crowd.
core_idea: Join in with the crowd, but on your own terms.

text: It is precisely in times of immunity from care that the soul should toughen itself beforehand for occasions of greater stress, and it is while Fortune is kind that it should fortify itself against her violence. In days of peace the soldier performs manœuvres, throws up earthworks with no enemy in sight, and wearies himself by gratuitous toil, in order that he may be equal to unavoidable toil. If you would not have a man flinch when the crisis comes, train him before it comes.
note: Preparing for hardship while life is calm

tags.when_helps: Someone in a calm stretch of life who wants to prepare themselves for harder times ahead.

display_text: It is precisely in times of immunity from care that the soul should toughen itself beforehand for occasions of greater stress, and it is while Fortune is kind that it should fortify itself against her violence. If you would not have a man flinch when the crisis comes, train him before it comes.
plain: Use calm, easy times to toughen your mind for hard ones, as soldiers drill in peacetime. If you don't want someone to flinch in a crisis, train them before it arrives.
core_idea: Prepare for hardship while times are good.

text: Similarly with fire; it does not matter how great is the flame, but what it falls upon. For solid timbers have repelled a very great fire; conversely, dry and easily inflammable stuff nourishes the slightest spark into a conflagration. So it is with anger, my dear Lucilius; the outcome of a mighty anger is madness, and hence anger should be avoided, not merely that we may escape excess, but that we may have a healthy mind.
note: Anger; how small provocations ignite an unready mind

tags.when_helps: Someone whose temper flares easily, wanting to understand why anger should be avoided for their own health.

display_text: Similarly with fire; it does not matter how great is the flame, but what it falls upon. For solid timbers have repelled a very great fire; conversely, dry and easily inflammable stuff nourishes the slightest spark into a conflagration. So it is with anger, my dear Lucilius; the outcome of a mighty anger is madness, and hence anger should be avoided, not merely that we may escape excess, but that we may have a healthy mind.
plain: A fire's damage depends on what it lands on: solid wood resists, dry tinder blazes. Anger works the same way; great anger ends in madness, so avoid anger altogether to keep your mind healthy.
core_idea: Avoid anger to keep a healthy mind.

text: Why wait until there is nothing left for you to crave? That time will never come. We hold that there is a succession of causes, from which fate is woven; similarly, you may be sure, there is a succession in our desires; for one begins where its predecessor ends. You have been thrust into an existence which will never of itself put an end to your wretchedness and your slavery. Withdraw your chafed neck from the yoke; it is better that it should be cut off once for all, than galled for ever.
note: Endless desire; deciding to step off the treadmill

tags.safety_reason: Read alone, an existence that won't end one's wretchedness plus a neck better 'cut off once for all' reads as approving ending one's life.
tags.when_helps: Not suitable for readers in distress; in context it urges leaving an endless chase of ambition.

display_text: Why wait until there is nothing left for you to crave? That time will never come. You have been thrust into an existence which will never of itself put an end to your wretchedness and your slavery. Withdraw your chafed neck from the yoke; it is better that it should be cut off once for all, than galled for ever.

text: If you retreat to privacy, everything will be on a smaller scale, but you will be satisfied abundantly; in your present condition, however, there is no satisfaction in the plenty which is heaped upon you on all sides. Would you rather be poor and sated, or rich and hungry? Prosperity is not only greedy, but it also lies exposed to the greed of others. And as long as nothing satisfies you, you yourself cannot satisfy others.
note: Choosing a simpler life over unsatisfying success

keywords: poor and sated or rich and hungry
tags.when_helps: Someone with plenty who still feels unsatisfied, weighing a quieter, simpler life.

display_text: If you retreat to privacy, everything will be on a smaller scale, but you will be satisfied abundantly; in your present condition, however, there is no satisfaction in the plenty which is heaped upon you on all sides. Would you rather be poor and sated, or rich and hungry? Prosperity is not only greedy, but it also lies exposed to the greed of others. And as long as nothing satisfies you, you yourself cannot satisfy others.
plain: In a quieter, private life you would have less but feel full; now you have plenty and are never satisfied. Would you rather be poor and content, or rich and hungry? Wealth is greedy and draws others' greed.
core_idea: Better poor and content than rich and hungry.

plain_judge.issue: Drops that while nothing satisfies you, you cannot satisfy others.

text: “You must reflect carefully beforehand with whom you are to eat and drink, rather than what you are to eat and drink. For a dinner of meats without the company of a friend is like the life of a lion or a wolf.”
note: Value of companionship; loneliness amid plenty

tags.when_helps: Someone eating alone or planning social life, reminded that company matters more than the menu.

display_text: “You must reflect carefully beforehand with whom you are to eat and drink, rather than what you are to eat and drink. For a dinner of meats without the company of a friend is like the life of a lion or a wolf.”
plain: Think harder about who you will eat and drink with than about what you will eat. A meal without a friend is the life of a lion or a wolf.
core_idea: Choose your companions more carefully than your food.

text: It is, however, a mistake to select your friend in the reception-hall or to test him at the dinner-table. The most serious misfortune for a busy man who is overwhelmed by his possessions is, that he believes men to be his friends when he himself is not a friend to them, and that he deems his favours to be effective in winning friends, although, in the case of certain men, the more they owe, the more they hate. A trifling debt makes a man your debtor; a large one makes him an enemy.
note: False friends; trying to buy friendship with favours

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone surprised that people they helped or lent to have turned cold, rethinking what friendship is.

display_text: It is, however, a mistake to select your friend in the reception-hall or to test him at the dinner-table. The most serious misfortune for a busy man who is overwhelmed by his possessions is, that he believes men to be his friends when he himself is not a friend to them, and that he deems his favours to be effective in winning friends, although, in the case of certain men, the more they owe, the more they hate. A trifling debt makes a man your debtor; a large one makes him an enemy.
plain: Don't pick friends among those who come to flatter you. A busy, wealthy man thinks people are his friends when he is no friend to them; a small debt makes someone owe you, a large one makes them hate you.
core_idea: Big favours can turn people into enemies.

plain_judge.issue: Recasts reception-hall choice as flatterers; drops the belief that favours win friends.

text: This, I say, is the highest duty and the highest proof of wisdom,—that deed and word should be in accord, that a man should be equal to himself under all conditions, and always the same. “But,” you reply, “who can maintain this standard?” Very few, to be sure; but there are some. It is indeed a hard undertaking, and I do not say that the philosopher can always keep the same pace. But he can always travel the same path.
note: Living by your words; consistency despite imperfection

tags.when_helps: Someone discouraged at not always living up to their values, who needs to know staying on the path is enough.

display_text: This, I say, is the highest duty and the highest proof of wisdom,—that deed and word should be in accord, that a man should be equal to himself under all conditions, and always the same. “But,” you reply, “who can maintain this standard?” Very few, to be sure; but there are some. It is indeed a hard undertaking, and I do not say that the philosopher can always keep the same pace. But he can always travel the same path.
plain: The highest mark of wisdom is that your actions match your words and you stay the same person in every situation. Few manage it, and no philosopher keeps the same pace always, but he can always walk the same path.
core_idea: Wisdom means your actions match your words.

text: You should lay hold, once for all, upon a single norm to live by, and should regulate your whole life according to this norm. Some men restrict themselves at home, but strut with swelling port before the public; such discordance is a fault, and it indicates a wavering mind which cannot yet keep its balance.
note: Integrity; being the same person in private and public

tags.when_helps: Someone who acts one way in public and another at home, wanting one consistent way to live.

display_text: You should lay hold, once for all, upon a single norm to live by, and should regulate your whole life according to this norm. Some men restrict themselves at home, but strut with swelling port before the public; such discordance is a fault, and it indicates a wavering mind which cannot yet keep its balance.
plain: Choose one standard to live by and run your whole life by it. People who live modestly at home but show off in public reveal an unsteady mind that hasn't found its balance.
core_idea: Live by one consistent standard everywhere.

text: Poverty will keep for you your true and tried friends; you will be rid of the men who were not seeking you for yourself, but for something which you have. Is it not true, however, that you should love poverty, if only for this single reason,—that it will show you those by whom you are loved? O when will that time come, when no one shall tell lies to compliment you!
note: Hard times reveal who truly loves you

tags.when_helps: Someone who lost money or status and saw friends fall away, finding that it revealed who truly cares.

display_text: Poverty will keep for you your true and tried friends; you will be rid of the men who were not seeking you for yourself, but for something which you have. Is it not true, however, that you should love poverty, if only for this single reason,—that it will show you those by whom you are loved? O when will that time come, when no one shall tell lies to compliment you!
plain: Poverty keeps your true friends and clears away those who wanted what you had. You might love it for that alone, since it shows who really loves you. When will no one flatter you with lies?
core_idea: Poverty reveals who truly loves you.

text: No man is born rich. Every man, when he first sees light, is commanded to be content with milk and rags. Such is our beginning, and yet kingdoms are all too small for us!
note: Contentment; how little we truly need

tags.when_helps: Someone never satisfied with what they have, reminded how little everyone starts with.

display_text: No man is born rich. Every man, when he first sees light, is commanded to be content with milk and rags. Such is our beginning, and yet kingdoms are all too small for us!
plain: Nobody is born rich. Every baby must make do with milk and rags; that is how we all start, and yet later whole kingdoms feel too small for us.
core_idea: We start with little, then want everything.

text: Your greatest difficulty is with yourself; for you are your own stumbling-block. You do not know what you want. You are better at approving the right course than at following it out. You see where the true happiness lies, but you have not the courage to attain it.
note: Being your own obstacle; indecision and lack of courage

tags.when_helps: Someone who knows what they should do but keeps not doing it, and suspects they are their own obstacle.

display_text: Your greatest difficulty is with yourself; for you are your own stumbling-block. You do not know what you want. You are better at approving the right course than at following it out. You see where the true happiness lies, but you have not the courage to attain it.
plain: Your biggest obstacle is yourself. You don't know what you want; you approve the right path more readily than you follow it; you see where real happiness lies but lack the courage to reach it.
core_idea: You are your own biggest obstacle.

text: The deep flood of time will roll over us; some few great men will raise their heads above it, and, though destined at the last to depart into the same realms of silence, will battle against oblivion and maintain their ground for long.
note: Mortality, legacy and being forgotten

tags.when_helps: Someone wondering whether anything they do will be remembered once time washes over everyone.

display_text: The deep flood of time will roll over us; some few great men will raise their heads above it, and, though destined at the last to depart into the same realms of silence, will battle against oblivion and maintain their ground for long.
plain: Time will sweep over us all like a flood. A few great people will keep their heads above it for a long while, fighting oblivion, though in the end they too will go into silence.
core_idea: Time buries all; a few resist longer.

text: “If you wish,” said he, “to make Pythocles rich, do not add to his store of money, but subtract from his desires.”
note: Wanting less as the path to enough

tags.when_helps: Someone who feels poor and thinks the answer is more money, rather than wanting less.

display_text: “If you wish,” said he, “to make Pythocles rich, do not add to his store of money, but subtract from his desires.”
plain: Epicurus said that to make Pythocles rich, you shouldn't give him more money but take away some of his desires.
core_idea: Wealth comes from wanting less, not having more.

text: Men complain about their ambitions as they complain about their mistresses; in other words, if you penetrate their real feelings, you will find, not hatred, but bickering. Search the minds of those who cry down what they have desired, who talk about escaping from things which they are unable to do without; you will comprehend that they are lingering of their own free will in a situation which they declare they find it hard and wretched to endure. It is so, my dear Lucilius; there are a few men whom slavery holds fast, but there are many more who hold fast to slavery.
note: Complaining about a situation you choose to stay in

tags.when_helps: Someone complaining endlessly about a job or ambition they claim to hate but won't leave.

display_text: Men complain about their ambitions as they complain about their mistresses; in other words, if you penetrate their real feelings, you will find, not hatred, but bickering. Search the minds of those who cry down what they have desired, who talk about escaping from things which they are unable to do without; you will comprehend that they are lingering of their own free will in a situation which they declare they find it hard and wretched to endure. It is so, my dear Lucilius; there are a few men whom slavery holds fast, but there are many more who hold fast to slavery.
plain: People complain about their ambitions the way lovers complain about each other: it is squabbling, not real hatred. They stay by choice in what they call unbearable. A few are held by slavery; many more cling to it.
core_idea: Many people cling to what they claim enslaves them.

text: But if you keep turning round and looking about, in order to see how much you may carry away with you, and how much money you may keep to equip yourself for the life of leisure, you will never find a way out. No man can swim ashore and take his baggage with him.
note: Making a real change means letting go

situations: a career change or new job
tags.when_helps: Someone wanting to leave a demanding life but holding on to keep every comfort, unable to make the break.

display_text: But if you keep turning round and looking about, in order to see how much you may carry away with you, and how much money you may keep to equip yourself for the life of leisure, you will never find a way out. No man can swim ashore and take his baggage with him.
plain: If you keep looking back to see how much wealth you can take with you into a quieter life, you will never get out. No one can swim to shore carrying their luggage.
core_idea: You can't escape while clutching your possessions.

text: Take anyone off his guard,—young, old, or middle-aged; you will find that all are equally afraid of death, and equally ignorant of life. No one has anything finished, because we have kept putting off into the future all our undertakings.
note: Procrastination and fear of death

tags.when_helps: Someone afraid of death who realises they have also kept postponing life.

display_text: Take anyone off his guard,—young, old, or middle-aged; you will find that all are equally afraid of death, and equally ignorant of life. No one has anything finished, because we have kept putting off into the future all our undertakings.
plain: Catch anyone unawares, young or old, and you will find them equally afraid of death and equally ignorant of how to live. No one has finished anything, because we keep postponing everything to the future.
core_idea: Postponing life leaves us afraid of death.

text: A man has caught the message of wisdom, if he can die as free from care as he was at birth; but as it is, we are all a-flutter at the approach of the dreaded end. Our courage fails us, our cheeks blanch; our tears fall, though they are unavailing. But what is baser than to fret at the very threshold of peace?
note: Facing death without dread

tags.safety_reason: Calls death 'the very threshold of peace' and treats fretting at it as base, presenting death as a release.
tags.when_helps: Someone calmly facing their own death who wants to meet it without fear.

display_text: A man has caught the message of wisdom, if he can die as free from care as he was at birth; but as it is, we are all a-flutter at the approach of the dreaded end. Our courage fails us, our cheeks blanch; our tears fall, though they are unavailing. But what is baser than to fret at the very threshold of peace?
plain: A person has understood wisdom if they can die as free of worry as when they were born. Instead we panic as the end nears, turning pale and weeping uselessly. What is worse than fretting at the doorway of peace?
core_idea: Wisdom is dying as calmly as you were born.

text: Men do not care how nobly they live, but only how long, although it is within the reach of every man to live nobly, but within no man’s power to live long.
note: Living well rather than merely long

tags.when_helps: Someone fixated on living longer who could shift focus to living well.

display_text: Men do not care how nobly they live, but only how long, although it is within the reach of every man to live nobly, but within no man’s power to live long.
plain: People care how long they live, not how well, though anyone can choose to live nobly and no one can choose to live long.
core_idea: Living nobly is in our power; living long isn't.

text: Do you ask what is the foundation of a sound mind? It is, not to find joy in useless things. I said that it was the foundation; it is really the pinnacle. We have reached the heights if we know what it is that we find joy in and if we have not placed our happiness in the control of externals. The man who is goaded ahead by hope of anything, though it be within reach, though it be easy of access, and though his ambitions have never played him false, is troubled and unsure of himself.
note: Happiness that does not depend on external things

tags.when_helps: Someone whose happiness depends on the next purchase or goal, feeling unsettled despite getting what they want.

display_text: Do you ask what is the foundation of a sound mind? It is, not to find joy in useless things. I said that it was the foundation; it is really the pinnacle. We have reached the heights if we know what it is that we find joy in and if we have not placed our happiness in the control of externals. The man who is goaded ahead by hope of anything, though it be within reach, though it be easy of access, and though his ambitions have never played him false, is troubled and unsure of himself.
plain: The foundation, and really the summit, of a sound mind is not taking joy in useless things and not letting outside things control your happiness. Anyone driven by hope for something, however attainable, stays troubled and unsure.
core_idea: Don't let external things control your happiness.

text: I do not wish you ever to be deprived of gladness. I would have it born in your house; and it is born there, if only it be inside of you. Other objects of cheer do not fill a man’s bosom; they merely smooth his brow and are inconstant,—unless perhaps you believe that he who laughs has joy. The very soul must be happy and confident, lifted above every circumstance.
note: Finding joy within rather than in distractions

tags.when_helps: Someone whose fun feels hollow, looking for a deeper gladness that comes from within.

display_text: I do not wish you ever to be deprived of gladness. I would have it born in your house; and it is born there, if only it be inside of you. Other objects of cheer do not fill a man’s bosom; they merely smooth his brow and are inconstant,—unless perhaps you believe that he who laughs has joy. The very soul must be happy and confident, lifted above every circumstance.
plain: I want you never to lack gladness, and for it to be born at home, inside you. Other pleasures only smooth the brow for a while; laughing isn't joy. The soul itself must be happy and confident, above every circumstance.
core_idea: Real gladness is born inside you.

text: Do you ask me what this real good is, and whence it derives? I will tell you: it comes from a good conscience, from honourable purposes, from right actions, from contempt of the gifts of chance, from an even and calm way of living which treads but one path. For men who leap from one purpose to another, or do not even leap but are carried over by a sort of hazard,—how can such wavering and unstable persons possess any good that is fixed and lasting?
note: Where lasting good comes from; steadiness of purpose

tags.when_helps: Someone jumping between goals who wants to know where lasting good actually comes from.

display_text: Do you ask me what this real good is, and whence it derives? I will tell you: it comes from a good conscience, from honourable purposes, from right actions, from contempt of the gifts of chance, from an even and calm way of living which treads but one path. For men who leap from one purpose to another, or do not even leap but are carried over by a sort of hazard,—how can such wavering and unstable persons possess any good that is fixed and lasting?
plain: Real good comes from a clear conscience, honourable aims, right actions, indifference to luck, and a calm, steady life on one path. People who jump from one goal to another, or drift by chance, cannot hold any lasting good.
core_idea: Lasting good comes from a steady, honest life.

text: There are only a few who control themselves and their affairs by a guiding purpose; the rest do not proceed; they are merely swept along, like objects afloat in a river. And of these objects, some are held back by sluggish waters and are transported gently; others are torn along by a more violent current; some, which are nearest the bank, are left there as the current slackens; and others are carried out to sea by the onrush of the stream. Therefore, we should decide what we wish, and abide by the decision.
note: Drifting through life; choosing a direction

keywords: swept along like objects in a river
tags.when_helps: Someone drifting through life without decisions of their own, ready to choose what they want and stick to it.

text: Why, indeed, is it necessary to summon trouble,—which must be endured soon enough when it has once arrived,—or to anticipate trouble and ruin the present through fear of the future? It is indeed foolish to be unhappy now because you may be unhappy at some future time. But I shall conduct you to peace of mind by another route: if you would put off all worry, assume that what you fear may happen will certainly happen in any event; whatever the trouble may be, measure it in your own mind, and estimate the amount of your fear. You will thus understand that what you fear is either insignificant or short-lived.
note: Anxiety about future outcomes; facing the worst case

keywords: assume the worst and measure it
tags.when_helps: Someone ruining today by dreading a future event, who could face the worst case squarely and size it.

text: Remember, however, before all else, to strip things of all that disturbs and confuses, and to see what each is at bottom; you will then comprehend that they contain nothing fearful except the actual fear. What you see happening to boys happens also to ourselves, who are only slightly bigger boys: when those whom they love, with whom they daily associate, with whom they play, appear with masks on, the boys are frightened out of their wits. We should strip the mask, not only from men, but from things, and restore to each object its own aspect.
note: Fear; seeing things as they really are

tags.when_helps: Someone frightened by how a situation looks, who could strip it down to see what is actually there.

text: What, have you only at this moment learned that death is hanging over your head, at this moment exile, at this moment grief? You were born to these perils. Let us think of everything that can happen as something which will happen.

text: I may become a poor man; I shall then be one among many. I may be exiled; I shall then regard myself as born in the place to which I shall be sent. They may put me in chains. What then? Am I free from bonds now? Behold this clogging burden of a body, to which nature has fettered me! “I shall die,” you say; you mean to say “I shall cease to run the risk of sickness; I shall cease to run the risk of imprisonment; I shall cease to run the risk of death.”
note: Facing feared losses calmly; reframing misfortune

tags.safety_reason: Recasts 'I shall die' as ceasing to risk sickness and imprisonment, presenting death as relief from life's burdens.

text: We lose our childhood, then our boyhood, and then our youth. Counting even yesterday, all past time is lost time; the very day which we are now spending is shared between ourselves and death. It is not the last drop that empties the water-clock, but all that which previously has flowed out; similarly, the final hour when we cease to exist does not of itself bring death; it merely of itself completes the death-process. We reach death at that moment, but we have been a long time on the way.
note: Ageing and mortality; time slipping away

tags.when_helps: Someone mourning lost youth, reflecting on how life passes drop by drop.

text: “Do everything as if Epicurus were watching you.” There is no real doubt that it is good for one to have appointed a guardian over oneself, and to have someone whom you may look up to, someone whom you may regard as a witness of your thoughts. It is, indeed, nobler by far to live as you would live under the eyes of some good man, always at your side; but nevertheless I am content if you only act, in whatever you do, as you would act if anyone at all were looking on; because solitude prompts us to all kinds of evil.
note: Self-discipline; living as if a good person were watching

situations: a habit or addiction I can't break
tags.when_helps: Someone who slips when nobody is around, looking for a way to hold themselves accountable.

text: Put aside the opinion of the world; it is always wavering and always takes both sides. Put aside the studies which you have pursued throughout your life; Death will deliver the final judgment in your case. This is what I mean: your debates and learned talks, your maxims gathered from the teachings of the wise, your cultured conversation,—all these afford no proof of the real strength of your soul. text: Of this one thing make sure against your dying day,—let your faults die before you die. Away with those disordered pleasures, which must be dearly paid for; it is not only those which are to come that harm me, but also those which have come and gone. Just as crimes, even if they have not been detected when they were committed, do not allow anxiety to end with them; so with guilty pleasures, regret remains even after the pleasures are over. They are not substantial, they are not trustworthy; even if they do not harm us, they are fleeting. Cast about rather for some good which will abide. But there can be no such good except as the soul discovers it for itself within itself. Virtue alone affords everlasting and peace-giving joy; even if some obstacle arise, it is but like an intervening cloud, which floats beneath the sun but never prevails against it.”

text: Socrates made the same remark to one who complained; he said: “Why do you wonder that globe-trotting does not help you, seeing that you always take yourself with you? Do you ask why such flight does not help you? It is because you flee along with yourself. You must lay aside the burdens of the mind; until you do this, no place will satisfy you.

text: I disagree with those who strike out into the midst of the billows and, welcoming a stormy existence, wrestle daily in hardihood of soul with life’s problems.
