text: Death belongs among those things which are not indeed evils, but still have in them a semblance of evil; for there are implanted in us love of self, a desire for existence and self-preservation, and also an abhorrence of dissolution, because death seems to rob us of many goods and to withdraw us from the abundance to which we have become accustomed. And there is another element which estranges us from death: we are already familiar with the present, but are ignorant of the future into which we shall transfer ourselves, and we shrink from the unknown. Moreover, it is natural to fear the world of shades, whither death is supposed to lead.
note: Why we naturally fear death and the unknown

tags.when_helps: Someone afraid of death, reassured that the fear is natural and understandable.

text: Besides, no deed that a man does is honourable unless he has devoted himself thereto and attended to it with all his heart, rebelling against it with no portion of his being. When, however, a man goes to face an evil, either through fear of worse evils or in the hope of goods whose attainment is of sufficient moment to him that he can swallow the one evil which he must endure,—in that case the judgment of the agent is drawn in two directions. On the one side is the motive which bids him carry out his purpose; on the other, the motive which restrains him and makes him flee from something which has aroused his apprehension or leads to danger. Hence he is torn in different directions; and if this happens, the glory of his act is gone. For virtue accomplishes its plans only when the spirit is in harmony with itself. There is no element of fear in any of its actions.
note: Being torn in two; acting wholeheartedly

tags.when_helps: Someone doing something hard while divided inside, wanting to act wholeheartedly.

text: Very soon does a wide interval open between two persons who travel different ways. My slave is climbing up at the very moment when I am coming down, and you surely know how much quicker the latter is. Nay, I was wrong; for now my life is not coming down; it is falling outright.

text: Lo, now the din of the Races sounds about me! My ears are smitten with sudden and general cheering. But this does not upset my thoughts or even break their continuity. text: Drunkenness kindles and discloses every kind of vice, and removes the sense of shame that veils our evil undertakings. For more men abstain from forbidden actions because they are ashamed of sinning than because their inclinations are good. When the strength of wine has become too great and has gained control over the mind, every lurking evil comes forth from its hiding-place. Drunkenness does not create vice, it merely brings it into view; at such times the lustful man does not wait even for the privacy of a bedroom, but without postponement gives free play to the demands of his passions; at such times the unchaste man proclaims and publishes his malady; at such times your cross-grained fellow does not restrain his tongue or his hand. The haughty man increases his arrogance, the ruthless man his cruelty, the slanderer his spitefulness. Every vice is given free play and comes to the front.
note: Drinking and loss of self-control

text: What glory is there in carrying much liquor? text: What then, you ask, is an evil? It is the yielding to those things which are called evils; it is the surrendering of one’s liberty into their control, when really we ought to suffer all things in order to preserve this liberty. Liberty is lost unless we despise those things which put the yoke upon our necks. If men knew what bravery was, they would have no doubts as to what a brave man’s conduct should be. For bravery is not thoughtless rashness, or love of danger, or the courting of fear-inspiring objects; it is the knowledge which enables us to distinguish between that which is evil and that which is not. Bravery takes the greatest care of itself, and likewise endures with the greatest patience all things which have a false appearance of being evils.

text: It was not of ivory only that Phidias knew how to make statues; he also made statues of bronze. If you had given him marble, or a still meaner material, he would have made of it the best statue that the material would permit. So the wise man will develop virtue, if he may, in the midst of wealth, or, if not, in poverty; if possible, in his own country—if not, in exile; if possible, as a commander—if not, as a common soldier; if possible, in sound health—if not, enfeebled. text: The vehicle in which I have taken my seat is a farmer’s cart. Only by walking do the mules show that they are alive. The driver is barefoot, and not because it is summer either. text: Do you raise the question, “Through what regions did Ulysses stray?” instead of trying to prevent ourselves from going astray at all times? We have no leisure to hear lectures on the question whether he was sea-tost between Italy and Sicily, or outside our known world (indeed, so long a wandering could not possibly have taken place within its narrow bounds); we ourselves encounter storms of the spirit, which toss us daily, and our depravity drives us into all the ills which troubled Ulysses. For us there is never lacking the beauty to tempt our eyes, or the enemy to assail us; on this side are savage monsters that delight in human blood, on that side the treacherous allurements of the ear, and yonder is shipwreck and all the varied category of misfortunes. Show me rather, by the example of Ulysses, how I am to love my country, my wife, my father, and how, even after suffering shipwreck, I am to sail toward these ends, honourable as they are.

Show me rather, by the example of Ulysses, how I am to love my country, my wife, my father, and how, even after suffering shipwreck, I am to sail toward these ends, honourable as they are.
plain: Why study where Ulysses wandered instead of how to keep ourselves from going astray? We face storms of the spirit daily. Show me instead how to love my country, wife and father, and sail toward them even after shipwreck.
core_idea: Study to live well, not for idle trivia

text: I, for my part, do not know what is to be, but I do know what may come to be. text: Nature was not so hostile to man that, when she gave all the other animals an easy rôle in life, she made it impossible for him alone to live without all these artifices. None of these was imposed upon us by her; none of them had to be painfully sought out that our lives might be prolonged. All things were ready for us at our birth; it is we that have made everything difficult for ourselves, through our disdain for what is easy. Houses, shelter, creature comforts, food, and all that has now become the source of vast trouble, were ready at hand, free to all, and obtainable for trifling pains. For the limit everywhere corresponded to the need; it is we that have made all those things valuable, we that have made them admired, we that have caused them to be sought for by extensive and manifold devices.

text: Do you ask what, then, the wise man has found out and what he has brought to light? First of all there is truth, and nature; and nature he has not followed as the other animals do, with eyes too dull to perceive the divine in it. In the second place, there is the law of life, and life he has made to conform to universal principles; and he has taught us, not merely to know the gods, but to follow them, and to welcome the gifts of chance precisely as if they were divine commands. He has forbidden us to give heed to false opinions, and has weighed the value of each thing by a true standard of appraisement. He has condemned those pleasures with which remorse is intermingled, and has praised those goods which will always satisfy; and he has published the truth abroad that he is most happy who has no need of happiness, and that he is most powerful who has power over himself.

text: The sun, however, is unimpaired even in the midst of obstacles, and, though an object may intervene and cut off our view thereof, the sun sticks to his work and goes on his course. Whenever he shines forth from amid the clouds, he is no smaller, nor less punctual either, than when he is free from clouds; since it makes a great deal of difference whether there is merely something in the way of his light or something which interferes with his shining. Similarly, obstacles take nothing away from virtue; it is no smaller, but merely shines with less brilliancy. In our eyes, it may perhaps be less visible and less luminous than before; but as regards itself it is the same and, like the sun when he is eclipsed, is still, though in secret, putting forth its strength. Disasters, therefore, and losses, and wrongs, have only the same power over virtue that a cloud has over the sun.

display_text: Now what is the chief thing in virtue? It is the quality of not needing a single day beyond the present, and of not reckoning up the days that are ours; in the slightest possible moment of time virtue completes an eternity of good.
plain: The heart of virtue is needing no day beyond today and not counting the days you have; in the briefest moment, virtue completes an eternity of good.
core_idea: Virtue needs nothing beyond the present moment

text: The soul, I affirm, knows that riches are stored elsewhere than in men’s heaped-up treasure-houses; that it is the soul, and not the strong-box, which should be filled.
note: True wealth is inner, not money

tags.when_helps: Someone chasing wealth who senses an emptiness possessions can't fill.

display_text: The soul, I affirm, knows that riches are stored elsewhere than in men’s heaped-up treasure-houses; that it is the soul, and not the strong-box, which should be filled.
plain: The soul knows that true riches are kept somewhere other than piled-up treasure houses: it is the soul, not the strongbox, that should be filled.
core_idea: Fill the soul, not the strongbox

text: But tell me, pray, do you consider it fairer that you should obey Nature, or that Nature should obey you? And what difference does it make how soon you depart from a place which you must depart from sooner or later? We should strive, not to live long, but to live rightly; for to achieve long life you have need of Fate only, but for right living you need the soul. A life is really long if it is a full life; but fulness is not attained until the soul has rendered to itself its proper Good, that is, until it has assumed control over itself.
note: Grief at early death; quality over length of life

tags.safety_reason: Asking what difference it makes how soon you depart could read to a distressed reader as indifference to dying early.
tags.when_helps: Someone grieving a life cut short or facing their own death, who wants to value a life by its fullness.

display_text: But tell me, pray, do you consider it fairer that you should obey Nature, or that Nature should obey you? And what difference does it make how soon you depart from a place which you must depart from sooner or later? We should strive, not to live long, but to live rightly; for to achieve long life you have need of Fate only, but for right living you need the soul. A life is really long if it is a full life; but fulness is not attained until the soul has rendered to itself its proper Good, that is, until it has assumed control over itself.
plain: Why does it matter how soon you leave a place you must leave anyway? Aim to live rightly, not long: long life needs only Fate, right living needs the soul. A life is long if it is full, through self-mastery.
core_idea: Live rightly rather than long

text: Pray, let us see to it, my dear Lucilius, that our lives, like jewels of great price, be noteworthy not because of their width but because of their weight. Let us measure them by their performance, not by their duration.
note: Measuring a life by its worth, not years

tags.when_helps: Someone worried their life is too short who wants to measure it by what it holds.

display_text: Pray, let us see to it, my dear Lucilius, that our lives, like jewels of great price, be noteworthy not because of their width but because of their weight. Let us measure them by their performance, not by their duration.
plain: Let our lives be like precious jewels, valued not for their size but for their weight. Measure them by what they achieve, not by how long they last.
core_idea: Measure life by its weight, not its length

text: Just as one of small stature can be a perfect man, so a life of small compass can be a perfect life. Age ranks among the external things. How long I am to exist is not mine to decide, but how long I shall go on existing in my present way is in my own control. This is the only thing you have the right to require of me,—that I shall cease to measure out an inglorious age as it were in darkness, and devote myself to living instead of being carried along past life.
note: A short life can be complete; truly living

tags.when_helps: Someone drifting through their days who wants to start truly living, whatever time remains.

display_text: Just as one of small stature can be a perfect man, so a life of small compass can be a perfect life. Age ranks among the external things. How long I am to exist is not mine to decide, but how long I shall go on existing in my present way is in my own control. This is the only thing you have the right to require of me,—that I shall cease to measure out an inglorious age as it were in darkness, and devote myself to living instead of being carried along past life.
plain: A short life can be a complete life, as a short person can be a complete person. How long I exist isn't mine to decide, but how I live is. I must stop drifting in darkness and truly live.
core_idea: How long you live isn't yours; how you live is

text: Death visits each and all; the slayer soon follows the slain. It is an insignificant trifle, after all, that people discuss with so much concern. And anyhow, what does it matter for how long a time you avoid that which you cannot escape?
note: Fear of death; mortality comes to all

tags.when_helps: Someone preoccupied with fear of death who needs it put in proportion.

display_text: Death visits each and all; the slayer soon follows the slain. It is an insignificant trifle, after all, that people discuss with so much concern. And anyhow, what does it matter for how long a time you avoid that which you cannot escape?
plain: Death comes to everyone; the killer soon follows the killed. It is a small thing that people worry about so much. And what does it matter how long you avoid what you cannot escape?
core_idea: Death comes to all; delay matters little

text: Remember that pain has this most excellent quality: if prolonged it cannot be severe, and if severe it cannot be prolonged; and that we should bravely accept whatever commands the inevitable laws of the universe lay upon us.
note: Enduring pain and accepting the inevitable

tags.when_helps: Someone living with pain who needs a steadying thought about how to bear it.

display_text: Remember that pain has this most excellent quality: if prolonged it cannot be severe, and if severe it cannot be prolonged; and that we should bravely accept whatever commands the inevitable laws of the universe lay upon us.
plain: Remember that pain has an excellent quality: if it lasts long it can't be severe, and if it is severe it can't last long. We should bravely accept whatever the unchanging laws of the universe demand of us.
core_idea: Severe pain is short; long pain is mild

text: The soul carries within itself the seed of everything that is honourable, and this seed is stirred to growth by advice, as a spark that is fanned by a gentle breeze develops its natural fire. Virtue is aroused by a touch, a shock.
note: Goodness already within us, awakened by guidance

tags.when_helps: Someone doubting there is any good in them, who needs to hear the seed is already there.

display_text: The soul carries within itself the seed of everything that is honourable, and this seed is stirred to growth by advice, as a spark that is fanned by a gentle breeze develops its natural fire. Virtue is aroused by a touch, a shock.
plain: The soul holds the seed of everything honourable, and advice stirs it to grow, as a gentle breeze fans a spark into flame. A touch, a jolt, is enough to rouse virtue.
core_idea: Good advice fans the seed of virtue within

text: Nothing is more successful in bringing honourable influences to bear upon the mind, or in straightening out the wavering spirit that is prone to evil, than association with good men. For the frequent seeing, the frequent hearing of them little by little sinks into the heart and acquires the force of precepts. We are indeed uplifted merely by meeting wise men; and one can be helped by a great man even when he is silent.
note: Choosing good company; being shaped by others

tags.when_helps: Someone wavering in their values who could be strengthened by spending time with good people.

display_text: Nothing is more successful in bringing honourable influences to bear upon the mind, or in straightening out the wavering spirit that is prone to evil, than association with good men. For the frequent seeing, the frequent hearing of them little by little sinks into the heart and acquires the force of precepts. We are indeed uplifted merely by meeting wise men; and one can be helped by a great man even when he is silent.
plain: Nothing improves the mind or steadies a wavering spirit like spending time with good people. Seeing and hearing them gradually sinks into the heart; meeting wise people lifts us, and a great person can help even in silence.
core_idea: Good company slowly shapes the heart

text: Virtue depends partly upon training and partly upon practice; you must learn first, and then strengthen your learning by action.
note: Growth needs both learning and practice

tags.when_helps: Someone who has learned much but struggles to put it into practice.

display_text: Virtue depends partly upon training and partly upon practice; you must learn first, and then strengthen your learning by action.
plain: Virtue comes partly from training and partly from practice: first learn, then strengthen what you've learned by acting on it.
core_idea: Learn first, then strengthen learning by action

text: There is no word which reaches our ears without doing us harm; we are injured both by good wishes and by curses. The angry prayers of our enemies instil false fears in us; and the affection of our friends spoils us through their kindly wishes. For this affection sets us a-groping after goods that are far away, unsure, and wavering, when we really might open the store of happiness at home.
note: Others' expectations pull us from contentment

tags.when_helps: Someone pulled by others' hopes and fears for them, who wants contentment with what's within reach.

display_text: There is no word which reaches our ears without doing us harm; we are injured both by good wishes and by curses. The angry prayers of our enemies instil false fears in us; and the affection of our friends spoils us through their kindly wishes. For this affection sets us a-groping after goods that are far away, unsure, and wavering, when we really might open the store of happiness at home.
plain: Every word we hear does some harm, whether curses or good wishes. Enemies' prayers plant false fears, and friends' kind wishes spoil us, sending us after distant, uncertain goods when happiness is in store at home.
core_idea: Happiness is found at home, not in distant goods

text: “You need not be envious of those whom the people call great and fortunate; applause need not disturb your composed attitude and your sanity of mind; you need not become disgusted with your calm spirit because you see a great man, clothed in purple, protected by the well-known symbols of authority; you need not judge the magistrate for whom the road is cleared to be any happier than yourself, whom his officer pushes from the road. If you would wield a command that is profitable to yourself, and injurious to nobody, clear your own faults out of the way.
note: Envy of the successful and powerful

tags.when_helps: Someone envying powerful, admired people and feeling small beside them.

display_text: You need not be envious of those whom the people call great and fortunate; applause need not disturb your composed attitude and your sanity of mind; you need not become disgusted with your calm spirit because you see a great man, clothed in purple, protected by the well-known symbols of authority; you need not judge the magistrate for whom the road is cleared to be any happier than yourself, whom his officer pushes from the road. If you would wield a command that is profitable to yourself, and injurious to nobody, clear your own faults out of the way.
plain: Don't envy those the crowd calls great, or let applause or a magistrate in purple disturb your calm; he is no happier than you. For a command that helps you and harms no one, clear away your own faults.
core_idea: Master your own faults rather than envy power

text: You need never believe that a man can become happy through the unhappiness of another.
note: Happiness cannot come from harming others

tags.when_helps: Someone tempted to seek gain or satisfaction at another person's expense.

display_text: You need never believe that a man can become happy through the unhappiness of another.
plain: Never believe that anyone can become happy through someone else's unhappiness.
core_idea: No one gains happiness from another's misery

text: It is a great part of health to have forsaken the counsellors of madness and to have fled far from a companionship that is mutually baneful.
note: Leaving toxic company

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone who has stepped away from harmful company and wonders whether they did right.

display_text: It is a great part of health to have forsaken the counsellors of madness and to have fled far from a companionship that is mutually baneful.
plain: A large part of health is having left behind those who advise madness and having fled far from company that harms everyone in it.
core_idea: Leaving harmful company is part of health

text: You can make us cease to crave, if you only make us cease to display. Ambition, luxury, and waywardness need a stage to act upon; you will cure all those ills if you seek retirement.
note: Craving fed by the need to be seen

tags.when_helps: Someone caught in display and ambition who might find relief in a quieter life.

display_text: You can make us cease to crave, if you only make us cease to display. Ambition, luxury, and waywardness need a stage to act upon; you will cure all those ills if you seek retirement.
plain: Stop showing off and you'll stop craving. Ambition, luxury and self-indulgence need a stage to perform on; withdraw from the crowd and you cure them all.
core_idea: Without an audience, craving fades

text: For these two things are, as it were, at opposite poles—good fortune and good sense; that is why we are wiser when in the midst of adversity. It is prosperity that takes away righteousness.
note: Adversity teaches wisdom; success can corrupt

tags.when_helps: Someone in hard times who might see that adversity is sharpening their good sense.

display_text: For these two things are, as it were, at opposite poles—good fortune and good sense; that is why we are wiser when in the midst of adversity. It is prosperity that takes away righteousness.
plain: Good fortune and good sense sit at opposite poles, which is why we are wiser in hard times. It is prosperity that takes away our goodness.
core_idea: Adversity makes us wiser; prosperity corrupts

text: We often want one thing and pray for another, not telling the truth even to the gods, while the gods either do not hearken, or else take pity on us.
note: Not being honest about what we want

keywords: want one thing, pray for another
tags.when_helps: Someone realising they haven't been honest, even with themselves, about what they really want.

display_text: We often want one thing and pray for another, not telling the truth even to the gods, while the gods either do not hearken, or else take pity on us.
plain: We often want one thing and pray for another, not telling the truth even to the gods, who either don't listen or take pity on us.
core_idea: We aren't honest even in our prayers

text: When people sit by the bedsides of their sick friends, we honour their motives. But when people do this for the purpose of attaining a legacy, they are like vultures waiting for carrion. The same act may be either shameful or honourable: the purpose and the manner make all the difference.
note: Motives matter more than actions

situations: caring for a sick or ageing relative
tags.when_helps: Someone questioning their own motives behind a seemingly good act.

display_text: When people sit by the bedsides of their sick friends, we honour their motives. The same act may be either shameful or honourable: the purpose and the manner make all the difference.
plain: We honour those who sit by a sick friend's bed, but those hoping for an inheritance are vultures waiting for carrion. The same act can be shameful or honourable; purpose and manner make all the difference.

text: And as this belief is, so will be our acts and our thoughts. As our acts and our thoughts are, so will our lives be.
note: Beliefs shape actions, and actions shape life

tags.when_helps: Someone reflecting on how their beliefs are shaping their actions and the life they lead.

display_text: And as this belief is, so will be our acts and our thoughts. As our acts and our thoughts are, so will our lives be.

core_idea: Beliefs shape actions, and actions shape lives

text: Life without ideals is erratic: as soon as an ideal is to be set up, doctrines begin to be necessary. I am sure you will admit that there is nothing more shameful than uncertain and wavering conduct, than the habit of timorous retreat.
note: Drifting without purpose; indecision

tags.when_helps: Someone wavering without guiding ideals who keeps backing away from commitment.

display_text: Life without ideals is erratic: as soon as an ideal is to be set up, doctrines begin to be necessary. I am sure you will admit that there is nothing more shameful than uncertain and wavering conduct, than the habit of timorous retreat.
plain: Life without ideals wanders aimlessly, and setting up an ideal requires principles. Nothing is more shameful than uncertain, wavering conduct and the habit of timidly backing away.

text: Would you win over the gods? Then be a good man. Whoever imitates them, is worshipping them sufficiently.
note: True worship is living a good life

tags.when_helps: Someone unsure how to please or honour the divine, who might find it is in being good.

display_text: Would you win over the gods? Then be a good man. Whoever imitates them, is worshipping them sufficiently.
plain: Do you want to win the gods' favour? Then be a good person. Whoever imitates the gods worships them enough.
core_idea: Be good: imitating the gods is worship

text: What a little thing it is not to harm one whom you ought to help! It is indeed worthy of great praise, when man treats man with kindness!
note: Kindness beyond merely avoiding harm

tags.when_helps: Someone reflecting on how they treat others and wanting to choose real kindness.

display_text: What a little thing it is not to harm one whom you ought to help! It is indeed worthy of great praise, when man treats man with kindness!
plain: How small a thing it is merely not to harm someone you ought to help! What truly deserves praise is when people treat each other with kindness.
core_idea: Not harming is little; kindness deserves praise

text: Nature produced us related to one another, since she created us from the same source and to the same end. She engendered in us mutual affection, and made us prone to friendships. She established fairness and justice; according to her ruling, it is more wretched to commit than to suffer injury. Through her orders, let our hands be ready for all that needs to be helped.
note: Our shared humanity and duty to help

keywords: worse to commit than suffer injury
tags.when_helps: Someone feeling disconnected from others who needs reminding we are made for mutual care.

display_text: Nature produced us related to one another, since she created us from the same source and to the same end. She engendered in us mutual affection, and made us prone to friendships. She established fairness and justice; according to her ruling, it is more wretched to commit than to suffer injury. Through her orders, let our hands be ready for all that needs to be helped.
plain: Nature made us kin, from one source for one end, and gave us affection and a bent for friendship. By her law, doing wrong is worse than suffering it. Let our hands be ready to help wherever help is needed.
core_idea: We are kin; doing wrong is worse than suffering it

text:
Let this verse be in your heart and on your lips:
I am a man; and nothing in man’s lot
Do I deem foreign to me. Let us possess things in common; for birth is ours in common. Our relations with one another are like a stone arch, which would collapse if the stones did not mutually support each other, and which is upheld in this very way.
note: Interdependence; we hold each other up

tags.when_helps: Someone feeling cut off who needs a sense of shared humanity holding everyone up together.

display_text:
Let this verse be in your heart and on your lips:
I am a man; and nothing in man’s lot
Do I deem foreign to me. Let us possess things in common; for birth is ours in common. Our relations with one another are like a stone arch, which would collapse if the stones did not mutually support each other, and which is upheld in this very way.
plain: Keep this in your heart: I am human, and nothing human is foreign to me. Let us share things, since we share birth. We are like the stones of an arch, which would fall without each other's support.

text: Let us banish rumour and set a value upon each thing, asking what it is and not what it is called.
note: Seeing things as they are, not reputation

display_text: Let us banish rumour and set a value upon each thing, asking what it is and not what it is called.
plain: Let us ignore gossip and value each thing by asking what it actually is, not what it is called.
core_idea: Judge things by what they are, not their name

text: Peace of mind is enjoyed only by those who have attained a fixed and unchanging standard of judgment; the rest of mankind continually ebb and flow in their decisions, floating in a condition where they alternately reject things and seek them. And what is the reason for this tossing to and fro? It is because nothing is clear to them, because they make use of a most unsure criterion—rumour. If you would always desire the same things, you must desire the truth.
note: Indecision and restlessness; finding steady values

tags.when_helps: Someone tossed back and forth by indecision and others' opinions who wants steady footing.

display_text: Peace of mind is enjoyed only by those who have attained a fixed and unchanging standard of judgment; the rest of mankind continually ebb and flow in their decisions, floating in a condition where they alternately reject things and seek them. And what is the reason for this tossing to and fro? It is because nothing is clear to them, because they make use of a most unsure criterion—rumour. If you would always desire the same things, you must desire the truth.
plain: Only those with a fixed standard of judgement have peace of mind; others drift back and forth, rejecting then seeking the same things, because they judge by rumour. If you want to desire the same things always, desire the truth.
core_idea: To want steadily, want the truth

text: Spite of all do you still chafe and complain, not understanding that, in all the evils to which you refer, there is really only one—the fact that you do chafe and complain? If you ask me, I think that for a man there is no misery unless there be something in the universe which he thinks miserable. I shall not endure myself on that day when I find anything unendurable.
note: Complaining makes hardship worse

tags.when_helps: Someone stuck in complaint who might see that the complaining itself is the heaviest burden.

display_text: Spite of all do you still chafe and complain, not understanding that, in all the evils to which you refer, there is really only one—the fact that you do chafe and complain? If you ask me, I think that for a man there is no misery unless there be something in the universe which he thinks miserable. I shall not endure myself on that day when I find anything unendurable.
plain: Of all the evils you complain about, the only real one is your complaining. There is no misery for a person unless he thinks something miserable. The day I find anything unbearable, I won't be able to bear myself.
core_idea: Complaining is the only real evil

text: I am ill; but that is a part of my lot. My slaves have fallen sick, my income has gone off, my house is rickety, I have been assailed by losses, accidents, toil, and fear; this is a common thing. Nay, that was an understatement; it was an inevitable thing.
note: Illness and losses are part of every life

tags.when_helps: Someone hit by illness, money trouble and losses at once, who needs to know this is part of life.

display_text: I am ill; but that is a part of my lot. My slaves have fallen sick, my income has gone off, my house is rickety, I have been assailed by losses, accidents, toil, and fear; this is a common thing. Nay, that was an understatement; it was an inevitable thing.
plain: I am ill, but that is part of my lot. My slaves are sick, my income is gone, my house is falling apart, and I have faced losses, accidents, work and fear. This is common; in fact, it is unavoidable.
core_idea: Troubles are a common, unavoidable part of life

text: If you will believe me, it is my inmost emotions that I am just now disclosing to you: when everything seems to go hard and uphill, I have trained myself not merely to obey God, but to agree with His decisions. I follow Him because my soul wills it, and not because I must. Nothing will ever happen to me that I shall receive with ill humour or with a wry face. I shall pay up all my taxes willingly. Now all the things which cause us to groan or recoil, are part of the tax of life—things, my dear Lucilius, which you should never hope and never seek to escape.
note: Accepting hardship willingly as life's tax

tags.when_helps: Someone finding life uphill who wants to accept hardship willingly rather than with resentment.

display_text: If you will believe me, it is my inmost emotions that I am just now disclosing to you: when everything seems to go hard and uphill, I have trained myself not merely to obey God, but to agree with His decisions. text: A long life includes all these troubles, just as a long journey includes dust and mud and rain.
note: Troubles come with a long life

tags.when_helps: Someone worn down by life's ordinary troubles who needs them put in proportion.

display_text: A long life includes all these troubles, just as a long journey includes dust and mud and rain.
plain: A long life includes all these troubles, just as a long journey includes dust, mud and rain.
core_idea: Long lives bring troubles, like mud on journeys

text: And yet life, Lucilius, is really a battle. For this reason those who are tossed about at sea, who proceed uphill and downhill over toilsome crags and heights, who go on campaigns that bring the greatest danger, are heroes and front-rank fighters; but persons who live in rotten luxury and ease while others toil, are mere turtle-doves—safe only because men despise them.
note: Life is a struggle; hardship over ease

tags.when_helps: Someone toiling through hardship who needs to see their struggle as honourable.

display_text: And yet life, Lucilius, is really a battle. For this reason those who are tossed about at sea, who proceed uphill and downhill over toilsome crags and heights, who go on campaigns that bring the greatest danger, are heroes and front-rank fighters; but persons who live in rotten luxury and ease while others toil, are mere turtle-doves—safe only because men despise them.
plain: Life is a battle. Those who brave the sea, steep crags and dangerous campaigns are heroes in the front ranks; those in rotten luxury while others toil are turtle-doves, safe only because people despise them.
core_idea: Life is a battle; idle luxury is contemptible

text: You are mistaken, my dear Lucilius, if you think that luxury, neglect of good manners, and other vices of which each man accuses the age in which he lives, are especially characteristic of our own epoch; no, they are the vices of mankind and not of the times. No era in history has ever been free from blame.
note: Despair about the times we live in

keywords: vices of mankind not of the times
tags.when_helps: Someone convinced their era is uniquely corrupt, who needs a longer view.

display_text: You are mistaken, my dear Lucilius, if you think that luxury, neglect of good manners, and other vices of which each man accuses the age in which he lives, are especially characteristic of our own epoch; no, they are the vices of mankind and not of the times. No era in history has ever been free from blame.
plain: You are wrong to think luxury, bad manners and other vices each generation blames on its age are special to our time. They are the vices of humanity, not of the era; no age has been free of blame.

text: We degenerate easily, because we lack neither guides nor associates in our wickedness, and the wickedness goes on of itself, even without guides or associates. The road to vice is not only downhill, but steep; and many men are rendered incorrigible by the fact that, while in all other crafts errors bring shame to good craftsmen and cause vexation to those who go astray, the errors of life are a positive source of pleasure.
note: How easily bad habits take hold

situations: a habit or addiction I can't break
tags.when_helps: Someone noticing how easily they slide into bad habits and how pleasant the slide feels.

display_text: We degenerate easily, because we lack neither guides nor associates in our wickedness, and the wickedness goes on of itself, even without guides or associates. The road to vice is not only downhill, but steep; and many men are rendered incorrigible by the fact that, while in all other crafts errors bring shame to good craftsmen and cause vexation to those who go astray, the errors of life are a positive source of pleasure.
plain: We slide into wrongdoing easily, with or without guides and companions. The road to vice is downhill and steep, and many become incurable because, unlike mistakes in a craft, the mistakes of life bring pleasure.
core_idea: The road to vice is steep and pleasant

text: A good conscience, however, wishes to come forth and be seen of men; wickedness fears the very shadows.

tags.when_helps: Someone hiding something they did who feels the weight of a troubled conscience.

display_text: A good conscience, however, wishes to come forth and be seen of men; wickedness fears the very shadows.
plain: A good conscience wants to come out and be seen, but wickedness is afraid even of shadows.
core_idea: A good conscience seeks light; guilt fears shadows

text: Good luck frees many men from punishment, but no man from fear. And why should this be if it were not that we have ingrained in us a loathing for that which Nature has condemned? Hence even men who hide their sins can never count upon remaining hidden; for their conscience convicts them and reveals them to themselves. But it is the property of guilt to be in fear.
note: Guilt and a troubled conscience

tags.when_helps: Someone who escaped consequences for a wrong yet can't escape the fear that came with it.

display_text: Good luck frees many men from punishment, but no man from fear. And why should this be if it were not that we have ingrained in us a loathing for that which Nature has condemned? plain: Good luck saves many from punishment, but no one from fear, because we loathe what Nature condemns. Those who hide their wrongs can never be sure of staying hidden; their conscience convicts them. Guilt always lives in fear.

text: You need never believe that anyone who depends upon happiness is happy! It is a fragile support—this delight in adventitious things; the joy which entered from without will some day depart. But that joy which springs wholly from oneself is leal and sound; it increases and attends us to the last; while all other things which provoke the admiration of the crowd are but temporary Goods. You may reply: “What do you mean? Cannot such things serve both for utility and for delight?” Of course. But only if they depend on us, and not we on them.

display_text: You need never believe that anyone who depends upon happiness is happy! It is a fragile support—this delight in adventitious things; the joy which entered from without will some day depart. text: All things that Fortune looks upon become productive and pleasant, only if he who possesses them is in possession also of himself, and is not in the power of that which belongs to him. text: What resource do we find, then, in the face of these losses? A man is thankless in the highest degree if, after losing something, he feels no obligation for having received it. text: Why have we been slack? Why do we lose heart? We may return to the true path; we may be restored to our proper state; let us therefore be so, in order that we may be able to endure pain, in whatever form it attacks our bodies, and say to Fortune: “You have to deal with a man; seek someone whom you can conquer!”

text: Periods of time separate us, but death levels us. All things are tossed about and shift into their opposites at the bidding of Fortune; amid such a turmoil of mortal affairs nothing but death is surely in store for anyone. text: We must get rid of this craving for life, and learn that it makes no difference when your suffering comes, because at some time you are bound to suffer. The point is, not how long you live, but how nobly you live. And often this living nobly means that you cannot live long.
note: quality of life over its length

tags.safety_reason: Urges getting rid of the craving for life, which could read to a distressed reader as devaluing staying alive.
tags.when_helps: Someone facing mortality who wants to value living well over living long.

display_text: We must get rid of this craving for life, and learn that it makes no difference when your suffering comes, because at some time you are bound to suffer. The point is, not how long you live, but how nobly you live. And often this living nobly means that you cannot live long.
plain: We must drop our craving for more life; suffering will come at some point anyway. What matters is not how long you live but how nobly, and living nobly often means not living long.
core_idea: How nobly you live matters, not how long

text: The human soul is a great and noble thing; it permits of no limits except those which can be shared even by the gods.

text: These delays of mortal existence are a prelude to the longer and better life. As the mother’s womb holds us for ten months, making us ready, not for the womb itself, but for the existence into which we seem to be sent forth when at last we are fitted to draw breath and live in the open; just so, throughout the years extending between infancy and old age, we are making ourselves ready for another birth. A different beginning, a different condition, await us. We cannot yet, except at rare intervals, endure the light of heaven; therefore, look forward without fearing to that appointed hour,—the last hour of the body but not of the soul. Survey everything that lies about you, as if it were luggage in a guest-chamber: you must travel on. Nature strips you as bare at your departure as at your entrance.
note: facing mortality; death as another birth

tags.safety_reason: Presents death as birth into a longer and better life, something to look forward to.
tags.when_helps: Someone facing their own death who finds comfort in seeing it as a passage rather than an end.

text: That day, which you fear as being the end of all things, is the birthday of your eternity.

tags.when_helps: Someone near the end of life who fears death as final and seeks a hopeful framing.

text: Why are you looking about for troubles which may perhaps come your way, but which may indeed not come your way at all? I mean fires, falling buildings, and other accidents of the sort that are mere events rather than plots against us. Rather beware and shun those troubles which dog our steps and reach out their hands against us. Accidents, though they may be serious, are few—such as being shipwrecked or thrown from one’s carriage; but it is from his fellow-man that a man’s everyday danger comes. Equip yourself against that; watch that with an attentive eye. There is no evil more frequent, no evil more persistent, no evil more insinuating.
note: worrying about unlikely disasters; harm from people

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone worrying about unlikely accidents who might redirect attention to real, everyday risks.

text: It gives proof of a great heart to return to life for the sake of others; and noble men have often done this. But this procedure also, I believe, indicates the highest type of kindness: that although the greatest advantage of old age is the opportunity to be more negligent regarding self-preservation and to use life more adventurously, one should watch over one’s old age with still greater care if one knows that such action is pleasing, useful, or desirable in the eyes of a person whom one holds dear.
note: caring for yourself for the sake of loved ones

tags.safety_reason: Calls neglecting self-preservation in old age an advantage and implies a choice about leaving life.

text: Socrates is reported to have replied, when a certain person complained of having received no benefit from his travels: “It serves you right! You travelled in your own company!” O what a blessing it would be for some men to wander away from themselves! As it is, they cause themselves vexation, worry, demoralization, and fear! What profit is there in crossing the sea and in going from one city to another? If you would escape your troubles, you need not another place but another personality. Perhaps you have reached Athens, or perhaps Rhodes; choose any state you fancy, how does it matter what its character may be? You will be bringing to it your own.
note: wanting to escape; problems travel with you

tags.when_helps: Someone hoping a move or trip will fix their unhappiness, when the trouble travels with them.

plain: Told that a man's travels did him no good, Socrates said he had taken himself along. To escape your troubles you need a new self, not a new place; wherever you go, you bring your own character.
core_idea: You can't escape your troubles by travelling

text: Suppose that you hold wealth to be a good: poverty will then distress you, and,—which is most pitiable,—it will be an imaginary poverty. For you may be rich, and nevertheless, because your neighbour is richer, you suppose yourself to be poor exactly by the same amount in which you fall short of your neighbour. You may deem official position a good; you will be vexed at another’s appointment or re-appointment to the consulship; you will be jealous whenever you see a name several times in the state records. Your ambition will be so frenzied that you will regard yourself last in the race if there is anyone in front of you.
note: envy and comparing yourself with others

tags.when_helps: Someone measuring themselves against richer or more successful peers and always feeling behind.

core_idea: Valuing wealth and status breeds endless envy

text: Even in the midst of safety you will have no confidence if your mind has once been given a shock; once it has acquired the habit of blind panic, it is incapable of providing even for its own safety. For it does not avoid danger, but runs away. Yet we are more exposed to danger when we turn our backs.

text: “New friends, however, will not be the same.” No, nor will you yourself remain the same; you change with every day and every hour. But in other men you more readily see what time plunders; in your own case the change is hidden, because it will not take place visibly. Others are snatched from sight; we ourselves are being stealthily filched away from ourselves. You will not think about any of these problems, nor will you apply remedies to these wounds. You will of your own volition be sowing a crop of trouble by alternate hoping and despairing. If you are wise, mingle these two elements: do not hope without despair, or despair without hope.
note: change, loss, and balancing hope with despair

tags.when_helps: Someone missing lost friends and swinging between hope and despair about the future.

text: There will be no benefit to you in this hurrying to and fro; for you are travelling with your emotions and are followed by your afflictions. Would that they were indeed following you! In that case, they would be farther away; as it is, you are carrying and not leading them. Hence they press about you on all sides, continually chafing and annoying you. It is medicine, not scenery, for which the sick man must go a-searching.

text: Nothing, however, will help you so much as keeping still—talking very little with others, and as much as may be with yourself. For there is a sort of charm about conversation, something very subtle and coaxing, which, like intoxication or love, draws secrets from us. No man will keep to himself what he hears. No one will tell another only as much as he has heard. And he who tells tales will tell names, too. Everyone has someone to whom he entrusts exactly what has been entrusted to him. Though he checks his own garrulity, and is content with one hearer, he will bring about him a nation, if that which was a secret shortly before becomes common talk.
note: gossip, secrets, and talking too much

text: The most important contribution to peace of mind is never to do wrong. Those who lack self-control lead disturbed and tumultuous lives; their crimes are balanced by their fears, and they are never at ease. For they tremble after the deed, and they are embarrassed; their consciences do not allow them to busy themselves with other matters, and continually compel them to give an answer. Whoever expects punishment, receives it, but whoever deserves it, expects it. Where there is an evil conscience something may bring safety, but nothing can bring ease; for a man imagines that, even if he is not under arrest, he may soon be arrested. His sleep is troubled; when he speaks of another man’s crime, he reflects upon his own, which seems to him not sufficiently blotted out, not sufficiently hidden from view. A wrongdoer sometimes has the luck to escape notice but never the assurance thereof.
note: guilty conscience and peace of mind

tags.when_helps: Someone whose peace is gone because of a wrong they did and fear being found out.

text: The programme of life is the same as that of a bathing establishment, a crowd, or a journey: sometimes things will be thrown at you, and sometimes they will strike you by accident. Life is not a dainty business. You have started on a long journey; you are bound to slip, collide, fall, become weary, and cry out: “O for Death!”—or in other words, tell lies. At one stage you will leave a comrade behind you, at another you will bury someone, at another you will be apprehensive. It is amid stumblings of this sort that you must travel out this rugged journey.
note: life's knocks and setbacks are normal

text: Everyone approaches courageously a danger which he has prepared himself to meet long before, and withstands even hardships if he has previously practised how to meet them. But, contrariwise, the unprepared are panic-stricken even at the most trifling things. We must see to it that nothing shall come upon us unforeseen. And since things are all the more serious when they are unfamiliar, continual reflection will give you the power, no matter what the evil may be, not to play the unschooled boy.
note: preparing the mind for hardship

tags.when_helps: Someone easily panicked who wants to prepare their mind ahead for hard things.

display_text: Everyone approaches courageously a danger which he has prepared himself to meet long before, and withstands even hardships if he has previously practised how to meet them. text: Winter brings on cold weather; and we must shiver. Summer returns, with its heat; and we must sweat. Unseasonable weather upsets the health; and we must fall ill. In certain places we may meet with wild beasts, or with men who are more destructive than any beasts. Floods, or fires, will cause us loss. And we cannot change this order of things; but what we can do is to acquire stout hearts, worthy of good men, thereby courageously enduring chance and placing ourselves in harmony with Nature.
note: accepting what cannot be changed

situations: loss of a home or something valued
tags.when_helps: Someone frustrated by misfortunes they can't change who wants to meet them with a stout heart.

A greedy man does good to none; he does
Most evil to himself.
plain: The poor lack many things; the greedy lack everything. A greedy person helps no one and harms himself most.
core_idea: Greed impoverishes and harms the greedy most

text: He needs but little who desires but little.
note: contentment with little

tags.when_helps: Someone who wants to need less and feel richer for it.

display_text: He needs but little who desires but little.
plain: Someone who wants little needs little.
core_idea: Want little and you need little

text:
The choicest days of hapless human life
Fly first; disease and bitter eld succeed,
And toil, till harsh death rudely snatches all.
note: ageing and the swift passing of youth

tags.when_helps: Someone feeling their best years slipping away as age approaches.

display_text:
The choicest days of hapless human life
Fly first; disease and bitter eld succeed,
And toil, till harsh death rudely snatches all.
plain: The best days of our unhappy human life go by first; then come sickness, bitter old age and toil, until harsh death takes everything away.
core_idea: Life's best days pass first

text: Just as the purest wine flows from the top of the jar and the thickest dregs settle at the bottom; so in our human life, that which is best comes first. Shall we allow other men to quaff the best, and keep the dregs for ourselves?
note: not wasting your best years

tags.when_helps: Someone wasting their prime years who needs urging to use them well.

display_text: Just as the purest wine flows from the top of the jar and the thickest dregs settle at the bottom; so in our human life, that which is best comes first. Shall we allow other men to quaff the best, and keep the dregs for ourselves?
plain: Just as the best wine pours from the top of the jar and the dregs sink to the bottom, the best part of life comes first. Should we let others drink the best and keep the dregs for ourselves?
core_idea: Life's best part comes first; don't waste it

text: Let us therefore strive with all courage, omitting attractions by the way; let us struggle with a single purpose, lest, when we are left behind, we comprehend too late the speed of quick-flying time, whose course we cannot stay. Let every day, as soon as it comes, be welcome as being the choicest, and let it be made our own possession.
note: making the most of each day

tags.when_helps: Someone distracted from what matters who wants to welcome and use each day.

display_text: Let us therefore strive with all courage, omitting attractions by the way; let us struggle with a single purpose, lest, when we are left behind, we comprehend too late the speed of quick-flying time, whose course we cannot stay. Let every day, as soon as it comes, be welcome as being the choicest, and let it be made our own possession.
plain: So let us work with courage and single purpose, skipping distractions, so we don't realise too late how fast time flies. Welcome each day as it comes as the best one, and make it truly yours.
core_idea: Welcome each day as the best and use it

plain_judge.issue: Drops 'when we are left behind' and that time's course cannot be stayed.

text: I shall show you how men can prove their words to be their own: it is by doing what they have been talking about.
note: living what you preach

tags.when_helps: Someone who talks about their values but struggles to act on them.

display_text: I shall show you how men can prove their words to be their own: it is by doing what they have been talking about.
plain: People prove their words are truly their own by doing what they talk about.
core_idea: Your words are yours when you act on them

text: Good men are mutually helpful; for each gives practice to the other’s virtues and thus maintains wisdom at its proper level. Each needs someone with whom he may make comparisons and investigations.
note: good friends help each other grow

tags.when_helps: Someone wanting companions who help them grow wiser and better.

display_text: Good men are mutually helpful; for each gives practice to the other’s virtues and thus maintains wisdom at its proper level. Each needs someone with whom he may make comparisons and investigations.
plain: Good people help each other, because each gives the other's virtues exercise and keeps wisdom sharp. Everyone needs someone to compare notes and think things through with.
core_idea: Good people sharpen each other's virtues

text: Moreover, it is in accordance with Nature to show affection for our friends, and to rejoice in their advancement as if it were absolutely our own. For if we have not done this, even virtue, which grows strong only through exercising our perceptions, will not abide with us. Now virtue advises us to arrange the present well, to take thought regarding the future, to deliberate and apply our minds; and one who takes a friend into council with him, can more easily apply his mind and think out his problem.
note: rejoicing in friends' success; seeking a friend's counsel

tags.when_helps: Someone celebrating a friend's success or seeking a friend's counsel on a hard choice.

display_text: Moreover, it is in accordance with Nature to show affection for our friends, and to rejoice in their advancement as if it were absolutely our own. For if we have not done this, even virtue, which grows strong only through exercising our perceptions, will not abide with us. Now virtue advises us to arrange the present well, to take thought regarding the future, to deliberate and apply our minds; and one who takes a friend into council with him, can more easily apply his mind and think out his problem.
plain: It is natural to love our friends and rejoice in their success as our own; without this, even virtue fades. Virtue asks us to plan and think carefully, and that is easier with a friend.
core_idea: Friendship strengthens virtue and clear thinking

plain_judge.issue: Compresses virtue's tasks; drops that virtue grows only through exercise.

text: They say that men see farther in the affairs of others than in their own. A defect of character causes this in those who are blinded by self-love, and whose fear in the hour of peril takes away their clear view of that which is useful; it is when a man is more at ease and freed from fear that he will begin to be wise.
note: seeing your own situation clearly

tags.when_helps: Someone too close to their own problem to see it clearly, clouded by fear.

display_text: They say that men see farther in the affairs of others than in their own. A defect of character causes this in those who are blinded by self-love, and whose fear in the hour of peril takes away their clear view of that which is useful; it is when a man is more at ease and freed from fear that he will begin to be wise.
plain: People see others' affairs more clearly than their own, because self-love blinds them and fear in danger clouds their judgment. Wisdom begins when a person is calm and free of fear.
core_idea: Wisdom begins when fear and self-love fall away

plain_judge.issue: Drops 'they say' framing and 'defect of character'; states as plain fact.

text: Apply careful investigation, considering how our affairs actually stand, and not what men say of them; you will then understand that evils are more likely to help us than to harm us. For how often has so-called affliction been the source and the beginning of happiness! How often have privileges which we welcomed with deep thanksgiving built steps for themselves to the top of a precipice, still uplifting men who were already distinguished—just as if they had previously stood in a position whence they could fall in safety!
note: misfortune that turns out well; risky good fortune

tags.when_helps: Someone hit by a setback who might see it as a possible turning point.

display_text: Apply careful investigation, considering how our affairs actually stand, and not what men say of them; you will then understand that evils are more likely to help us than to harm us. For how often has so-called affliction been the source and the beginning of happiness! How often have privileges which we welcomed with deep thanksgiving built steps for themselves to the top of a precipice, still uplifting men who were already distinguished—just as if they had previously stood in a position whence they could fall in safety!
plain: Look at how things really are, not how people describe them, and you'll see that misfortunes help us more than they harm us. Hardship has often started happiness, while welcomed privileges have often led people to a cliff edge.
core_idea: Misfortune often helps more than it harms

plain_judge.issue: 'More likely to help' firmed to 'help more'; precipice image thinned.

text: If, however, you are wise, measure all things according to the state of man; restrict at the same time both your joys and your fears. Moreover, it is worth while not to rejoice at anything for long, so that you may not fear anything for long.
note: moderating highs and lows

tags.when_helps: Someone riding emotional highs and lows who wants a more even keel.

display_text: If, however, you are wise, measure all things according to the state of man; restrict at the same time both your joys and your fears. Moreover, it is worth while not to rejoice at anything for long, so that you may not fear anything for long.
plain: If you are wise, measure everything by the human condition and limit both your joys and your fears. Don't rejoice in anything for long, so you won't fear anything for long.
core_idea: Limit joy so you limit fear

text: There is no reason why you should suppose that anything is to be feared. All these things which stir us and keep us a-flutter, are empty things. None of us has sifted out the truth; we have passed fear on to one another; none has dared to approach the object which caused his dread, and to understand the nature of his fear—aye, the good behind it. That is why falsehood and vanity still gain credit—because they are not refuted.
note: examining fears instead of passing them on

tags.when_helps: Someone gripped by fears they have never looked at closely.

display_text: There is no reason why you should suppose that anything is to be feared. All these things which stir us and keep us a-flutter, are empty things. None of us has sifted out the truth; we have passed fear on to one another; none has dared to approach the object which caused his dread, and to understand the nature of his fear—aye, the good behind it. That is why falsehood and vanity still gain credit—because they are not refuted.
plain: There is no reason to think anything is truly fearful; the things that unsettle us are empty. We pass fear to each other without ever examining what we dread, so falsehood survives because no one challenges it.
core_idea: Our fears are empty because we never examine them

plain_judge.issue: Drops 'the good behind it' and that no one has sifted out the truth.

text:
Like boys who cower frightened in the dark,
So grown-ups in the light of day feel fear.
note: irrational adult fears

tags.when_helps: An adult embarrassed by their fears who might feel less alone in them.

display_text:
Like boys who cower frightened in the dark,
So grown-ups in the light of day feel fear.
plain: Just as children cower in fear in the dark, grown adults feel afraid even in broad daylight.
core_idea: Adults fear in daylight as children fear the dark

text: What is necessary will meet you everywhere; what is superfluous has always to be hunted out—and with great endeavour.
note: needs versus wants

tags.when_helps: Someone wearing themselves out chasing extras when what they need is already close.

display_text: What is necessary will meet you everywhere; what is superfluous has always to be hunted out—and with great endeavour.
plain: What you truly need is found everywhere; what you don't need always has to be hunted down with great effort.
core_idea: Necessities are easy; luxuries take effort

text: Turn thyself rather to the true riches. Learn to be content with little, and cry out with courage and with greatness of soul: ‘We have water, we have porridge; let us compete in happiness with Jupiter himself.’ And why not, I pray thee, make this challenge even without porridge and water? For it is base to make the happy life depend upon silver and gold, and just as base to make it depend upon water and porridge.
note: happiness not dependent on possessions

tags.when_helps: Someone with little money who wants to find happiness not tied to wealth.

display_text: Turn thyself rather to the true riches. Learn to be content with little, and cry out with courage and with greatness of soul: ‘We have water, we have porridge; let us compete in happiness with Jupiter himself.’ And why not, I pray thee, make this challenge even without porridge and water? For it is base to make the happy life depend upon silver and gold, and just as base to make it depend upon water and porridge.
plain: Turn to true riches: learn to be content with little, and boldly say that with water and porridge you could rival Jupiter in happiness. Better still, need not even those, since happiness shouldn't depend on gold or on porridge.
core_idea: Happiness should depend on nothing external

plain_judge.issue: 'Base' softened to 'shouldn't'; challenge rendered as command.

text: If you are willing to think often of these things, you will strive not to seem happy, but to be happy, and, in addition, to seem happy to yourself rather than to others.
note: real happiness versus appearing happy

tags.when_helps: Someone performing happiness for others while feeling hollow inside.

display_text: If you are willing to think often of these things, you will strive not to seem happy, but to be happy, and, in addition, to seem happy to yourself rather than to others.
plain: If you think on these things often, you will try not to look happy but to be happy, and to seem happy to yourself rather than to others.
core_idea: Be happy, not merely seem happy

text: Men love and hate their vices at the same time.
note: mixed feelings about bad habits

situations: a habit or addiction I can't break
tags.when_helps: Someone torn between wanting to quit a bad habit and still being drawn to it.

display_text: Men love and hate their vices at the same time.
plain: People love and hate their own vices at the same time.
core_idea: We love and hate our vices at once

text: And what is Bravery? It is the impregnable fortress for our mortal weakness; when a man has surrounded himself therewith, he can hold out free from anxiety during life’s siege; for he is using his own strength and his own weapons.
note: courage as protection against anxiety

tags.when_helps: A reader who feels besieged by worries and wants to find their own inner strength to hold out.

display_text: And what is Bravery? It is the impregnable fortress for our mortal weakness; when a man has surrounded himself therewith, he can hold out free from anxiety during life’s siege; for he is using his own strength and his own weapons.
plain: Bravery is an unbreakable fortress for our human weakness. Someone protected by it can endure life's siege without anxiety, because they rely on their own strength and their own weapons.
core_idea: Bravery is a fortress for human weakness

text: At this point I would quote you a saying of our philosopher Posidonius: “There are never any occasions when you need think yourself safe because you wield the weapons of Fortune; fight with your own! Fortune does not furnish arms against herself; hence men equipped against their foes are unarmed against Fortune herself.”
note: relying on inner strength, not external advantages

tags.when_helps: Someone relying on money, status or luck for security, who senses it could vanish.

display_text: At this point I would quote you a saying of our philosopher Posidonius: “There are never any occasions when you need think yourself safe because you wield the weapons of Fortune; fight with your own! Fortune does not furnish arms against herself; hence men equipped against their foes are unarmed against Fortune herself.”
plain: Posidonius said you are never safe relying on weapons fortune gave you; fight with your own. Fortune never arms you against herself, so those armed against enemies are defenseless against fortune.
core_idea: Rely on inner strength, not fortune's gifts

text: Alexander, to be sure, harried and put to flight the Persians, the Hyrcanians, the Indians, and all the other races that the Orient spreads even to the Ocean; but he himself, as he slew one friend or lost another, would lie in the darkness lamenting sometimes his crime, and sometimes his loss; he, the conqueror of so many kings and nations, was laid low by anger and grief! For he had made it his aim to win control over everything except his emotions.
note: outward success without mastering emotions

tags.when_helps: An outwardly successful person whose anger or grief keeps overpowering them despite every achievement.

display_text: Alexander, to be sure, harried and put to flight the Persians, the Hyrcanians, the Indians, and all the other races that the Orient spreads even to the Ocean; but he himself, as he slew one friend or lost another, would lie in the darkness lamenting sometimes his crime, and sometimes his loss; he, the conqueror of so many kings and nations, was laid low by anger and grief! For he had made it his aim to win control over everything except his emotions.
plain: Alexander conquered nation after nation, yet he lay in the dark lamenting a friend he killed or lost, beaten by anger and grief. He aimed to control everything except his own emotions.
core_idea: Conquering the world isn't conquering yourself

text: Oh with what great mistakes are men obsessed, who desire to push their limits of empire beyond the seas, who judge themselves most prosperous when they occupy many provinces with their soldiery and join new territory to the old! Little do they know of that kingdom which is on an equality with the heavens in greatness! Self-Command is the greatest command of all.
note: ambition versus self-mastery

tags.when_helps: An ambitious reader always chasing more territory or status, ready to look inward instead.

display_text: Oh with what great mistakes are men obsessed, who desire to push their limits of empire beyond the seas, who judge themselves most prosperous when they occupy many provinces with their soldiery and join new territory to the old! Little do they know of that kingdom which is on an equality with the heavens in greatness! Self-Command is the greatest command of all.
plain: People are badly mistaken who think they prosper by conquering ever more territory. They know nothing of the kingdom as great as the heavens: command over yourself is the greatest command of all.
core_idea: Self-command is the greatest command

text: Let each man convince himself of this before all else—“I must be just without reward.” And that is not enough; let him convince himself also of this: “May I take pleasure in devoting myself of my own free will to uphold this noblest of virtues.” Let all his thoughts be turned as far as possible from personal interests. You need not look about for the reward of a just deed; a just deed in itself offers a still greater return.
note: doing right without expecting reward

tags.when_helps: Someone doing the right thing and feeling bitter that nobody rewards or notices it.

display_text: Let each man convince himself of this before all else—“I must be just without reward.” And that is not enough; let him convince himself also of this: “May I take pleasure in devoting myself of my own free will to uphold this noblest of virtues.” Let all his thoughts be turned as far as possible from personal interests. You need not look about for the reward of a just deed; a just deed in itself offers a still greater return.
plain: Everyone should first be convinced that they must be just without reward, and should even take pleasure in freely upholding justice. Don't look for a reward for doing right; the just act itself pays more.
core_idea: A just act is its own reward

plain_judge.issue: Drops turning thoughts away from personal interest.

text: Those who wish their virtue to be advertised are not striving for virtue but for renown. Are you not willing to be just without being renowned? Nay, indeed you must often be just and be at the same time disgraced. And then, if you are wise, let ill repute, well won, be a delight.
note: doing right when unrecognised or misjudged

tags.when_helps: A person criticised or disgraced for doing what they believe is right.

display_text: Those who wish their virtue to be advertised are not striving for virtue but for renown. Are you not willing to be just without being renowned? Nay, indeed you must often be just and be at the same time disgraced. And then, if you are wise, let ill repute, well won, be a delight.
plain: Those who want their virtue noticed are after fame, not virtue. You must be willing to be just without praise, often even while disgraced; if you are wise, take delight in a bad name earned by doing right.
core_idea: Be just without needing recognition

text: We should be sensible, and our wants more reasonable, if each of us were to take stock of himself, and to measure his bodily needs also, and understand how little he can consume, and for how short a time! But nothing will give you so much help toward moderation as the frequent thought that life is short and uncertain here below; whatever you are doing, have regard to death.
note: Excess and wanting more; mortality as a guide to moderation

tags.when_helps: Someone caught up in wanting more who could use the perspective of life's shortness.

display_text: We should be sensible, and our wants more reasonable, if each of us were to take stock of himself, and to measure his bodily needs also, and understand how little he can consume, and for how short a time! But nothing will give you so much help toward moderation as the frequent thought that life is short and uncertain here below; whatever you are doing, have regard to death.
plain: We'd want less if we saw how little we can consume and for how short a time. Nothing helps moderation more than remembering that life is short and uncertain; whatever you do, keep death in mind.
core_idea: Remembering death teaches moderation

text: What tears and toil does money wring from us! Greed is wretched in that which it craves and wretched in that which it wins! Think besides of the daily worry which afflicts every possessor in proportion to the measure of his gain! The possession of riches means even greater agony of spirit than the acquisition of riches. And how we sorrow over our losses—losses which fall heavily upon us, and yet seem still more heavy! And finally, though Fortune may leave our property intact, whatever we cannot gain in addition, is sheer loss!
note: Money worries and greed never feeling satisfied

tags.when_helps: A reader consumed by worry about money, whether gaining it, keeping it or losing it.

display_text: What tears and toil does money wring from us! Greed is wretched in that which it craves and wretched in that which it wins! Think besides of the daily worry which afflicts every possessor in proportion to the measure of his gain! The possession of riches means even greater agony of spirit than the acquisition of riches. And how we sorrow over our losses—losses which fall heavily upon us, and yet seem still more heavy! And finally, though Fortune may leave our property intact, whatever we cannot gain in addition, is sheer loss!
plain: Money costs us tears and toil. Greed is miserable both in craving and in getting; owning wealth brings more anguish than gaining it, losses hurt more than they should, and whatever we fail to add feels like loss.
core_idea: Wealth brings more misery than it relieves

plain_judge.issue: Drops 'though Fortune leave our property intact'.

text: Would that those who are bound to crave wealth could compare notes with the rich man! Would that those who are bound to seek political office could confer with ambitious men who have reached the most sought-after honours! They would then surely alter their prayers, seeing that these grandees are always gaping after new gain, condemning what is already behind them. For there is no one in the world who is contented with his prosperity, even if it comes to him on the run. Men complain about their plans and the outcome of their plans; they always prefer what they have failed to win.
note: Envy of the successful; success never brings contentment

tags.when_helps: Someone envying the rich or powerful, or who reached a goal and still feels unsatisfied.

display_text: Would that those who are bound to crave wealth could compare notes with the rich man! core_idea: No one is satisfied by what they win

plain_judge.issue: Drops complaints about plans and outcomes; 'even if it comes on the run'.

text: There is no vice which lacks some plea; there is no vice that at the start is not modest and easily entreated; but afterwards the trouble spreads more widely. If you allow it to begin, you cannot make sure of its ceasing. Every emotion at the start is weak. Afterwards, it rouses itself and gains strength by progress; it is more easy to forestall it than to forgo it.
note: Bad habits and emotions grow if not checked early

situations: a habit or addiction I can't break
tags.when_helps: A person feeling a small temptation or emotion starting, before it takes hold.

display_text: There is no vice which lacks some plea; there is no vice that at the start is not modest and easily entreated; but afterwards the trouble spreads more widely. If you allow it to begin, you cannot make sure of its ceasing. Every emotion at the start is weak. Afterwards, it rouses itself and gains strength by progress; it is more easy to forestall it than to forgo it.
